[h2]I Don't get It[/h2]

I don't think I understand the point of the game. It was investing and enjoyable but I felt confused a lot of the time. The way that the memory time-travel device works doesn't make sense to me. I didn't care about whether it made sense during Act 1, even though the game was trying to explain it to me. But after Act 1 it felt like I needed to get it to understand the story. And at the end I was left doing things that I didn't understand.

[spoiler]At first I hated the mechanics and thought the art style was boring, but I got used to them and really enjoyed Act 1. I was invested in the story and found the backwards storytelling interesting. But the story gets taken over by time-travel memory link stuff that was confusing and took away from the weight of the story. Suddenly there was a different "what could have been" plotline that I didn't understand the point of. If the story had ended when I discovered the reason Johnny doesn't remember I think I would have been satisfied.

I loved the music, and the story was investing; it could have been simpler though. the movement was annoying but there were many fun and interesting moments.

I don't know why the game even tries to explain the logistics of the time-travel memory stuff, especially if I ended up confused anyways. It reminded me of when horror movies try to come up with a supernatural backstory for the monster instead of just letting it exist and be scary. The game could have told me that I need memory links to go back in Johnny's memories and I wouldn't have needed more than that. i don't care about the more complicated function of the machine. I guess the story wouldn't have existed without the explanation. And if the machine was explained as little as I'm suggesting then what is the point of backwards storytelling? It still would have been interesting I feel. So my main complaint is that I don't understand what the game is trying to say about memory.

Also Act 1 confused me with the discussion of River's "condition." It seemed important and I thought a major revelation was coming but it was never mentioned after Act 1. I think I know what the condition is. Maybe the point was just representation; I did find River relatable. But the story treats the "condition" in a weird way that gives it so much weight. It is kind of treated like a terminal illness that will change the course of her life and the way everyone around her is able too relate to her when the "condition" is just that she thinks a bit differently from what is considered the norm.[/spoiler]

It is hard for me to tell how clever the creators of this game were being. I'm just confused. I enjoyed it though

I picked this one up because it was mentioned in my Video Game Design course quite a few times last year. It was brought up as a positive example of storytelling in games, and how a strong narrative can carry the entire experience without needing much in the way of traditional gameplay. I hadn’t played it before, so I wanted to give it a go.

This game is about two doctors travelling through a dying man’s memories to help him fulfil his final wish to go to the moon. You’re navigating through his past, one memory at a time, trying to figure out why that wish matters to him and how to make it feel real before he passes away. There’s a bit of time pressure (on the characters, not the player), which leads to some questionable decisions, which I found pretty shocking in the moment. That's how emotionally invested I was. =) Otherwise the game is charming, sometimes funny, and quietly sad.

There is a puzzle element to the game, but it’s very simple. Before you can jump to the next memory, you need to discover and prepare a “memento”. Activating each memento involves solving a small tile-flipping puzzle. They’re quick and easy, not really meant to challenge you as such. They feel more like little breaks between key scenes to slow the pacing and give you a moment to take everything in.

The narrative is definitely the focus here, not the gameplay. So if you’re into story-heavy games that lean more toward telling a good story than testing out your hand dexterity (mine's awful anyways), this is a must play. Sometimes I just need to play something super chill like this, even if it might make you a little teary-eyed. It’s not long, but it left a nice impression.

I already own a couple of the follow-up games, so I’ll be playing those at a later time.

To the Moon is one of those rare games whose reputation precedes it, a supposedly devastating emotional journey wrapped in the aesthetics of a retro RPG. And while some of the praise is absolutely warranted, approaching it with clear eyes reveals both its brilliance and its limitations.

Narratively, it’s a quietly ambitious piece. The premise - two scientists diving through a dying man’s memories to fulfill his final wish - is undeniably compelling, and when the story lands, it lands with a thud straight to the heart. The writing has an earnest, almost handmade quality: sentimental but not manipulative, quirky without tipping into outright cutesiness. The relationship at the story’s center is layered, messy, believable, and the final act is genuinely affecting.

Mechanically, though, To the Moon is barely a “game”. Interaction is extremely shallow: light exploration, trivial puzzles and the occasional connective mini-game that feels more like padding than meaningful engagement. The experience succeeds in spite of its mechanics, not because of them. Some jokes also overstay their welcome, and the script leans heavily on quirk as a way to smooth over pacing dips.

But even with those caveats, the emotional core is potent. The soundtrack is exquisite: simple piano themes that burrow under your skin and elevate every moment. The pixel art, though modest, supports the tone with warmth and clarity.

To the Moon isn’t flawless and it’s not the transcendent masterpiece some describe. It’s a touching, sincere narrative experience with rough edges and a remarkable heart; more interactive novella than traditional game. If you meet it on its own terms, it rewards you with something gentle, human and quietly unforgettable.

To The Moon is a game I remember watching Pewdiepie play like, over a decade ago, but I had no real memory of what the story was or anything besides its introductory premise. Overall, I really enjoyed most if not all the aspects of this game that it presents itself as. It is able to balance itself between being a lighthearted and emotional human experience of a story of how love drives our existence, while also exploring more psychological affects like trauma, mental disabilities, and finding meaning in life. In some sense though, I wish the game treated mental disabilities with some more tact instead of utilizing the mystery behind them for senseless psychological horror.

I will admit that I'm jaded from playing way more RPG Maker games before completing To The Moon, but its age and technical limitations are extremely apparent when playing. Decisions from what the controls were on keyboard, the lack of any options, and children-level puzzles are what diminish this game's overall experience. It is unfortunately a short game because you're forced to walk for a lot of it, and the wide and detailed environments often lacked optional interactions for the many objects present. [i]Despite this[/i], the game has amazing emotional moments and was able to build up to it meaningfully; it was mostly near the last half-hour, but I had some tears in my eyes like three separate times.

This game feels foundational if you want to broaden your horizons for story games, but I struggle to say it definitively is. It's a short game regardless, and I think the story is broadly appealing for most people, but it has good moments. Pick it up if you like love stories.

The idea of a company offering a service that consists of manipulating your memories through the use of technology in order to give you experiences you didn't actually have or forget those you had is not exactly new. Decades ago I read a short story by Phlip K. D*ck (the guy's last name is censored, WTF) called "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" that dealt with such a concept, and that would years later be adapted almost beyond recognition to film as Arnold Schwarzennegger's "Total Recall"  (later remade again). The film "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" is also about a similar concept. 

But what if you told a story about such a company but not focusing on the client having their memories modified, but on the actual technicians/specialists doing the job and that job consists on giving a dying person fake memories that grant a life-long wish or resolve a life-long regret? That's basically what this game is, packaged in retro pixel art and injected with enough humor and sincerity to make the emotional beats pay off. 

Stuff like this proves that a good story that is told effectively can make a very simple game with retro graphics hit as hard as any modern offering with complicated gameplay and mind-blowing hyper-realistic visuals.

Edit: The two mini-sodes centerd around the office's Christmas party further develop the company and Neil and Eva's characters and relationship, though they hint at something not being exactly what it seems. I especially liked the detail about people protesting outside the building because they disapprove of the service they provide. Seemed oddly realistic.

Plot-wise, I can't say much. Basically, you're a pair of scientists trying to grant an old mans wish as he lay on his deathbed. This is done by stepping through memories of his life. 

Mechanically, it's kind of questionable. To make progress you need to find "Memories Triggers"  hidden through each small memory. This might be looking at a backpack, walking to a certain place talking to a certain person etc. I think it's an excuse to have you explore each memory to take in the overall plot. Spinkle in a few minigames here and there and you've got the game.

I did have some issues with the overall pacing.  Yeah, it took me under 3 and a half hours... but it still felt a little long. Act 1 in particular felt like it took too long. There were 15+ stages of his life you work through, with at least a few that seemed unneeded. 

But I suspect my complaint is specifically because of the game play mechanics. Acts 2 and 3 rarely required memory triggers and felt like it flowed a lot faster. I enjoyed this late game experience far more than the second half of Act 1. 

Overall, I can't say the story worked for me the way it seems to have for others. But I at least did have plenty of feels and in the world game writing that makes it well-above average. There was some cheese, some decent jokes, some warm feelings, some sad ones, and a couple interesting twists.

I especially enjoyed the witty exchanges between Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts—they added a nice dose of humour to the heartfelt plot. The atmosphere also fits the story perfectly, enhancing the emotional impact.

However, the controls were a major downside for me. Most of the game is controlled with the mouse, and I found the movement clunky and awkward. It often pulled me out of the experience, which was disappointing given how immersive the story is. There’s also a horse-riding segment that uses arrow keys, but it’s surprisingly frustrating—the horse randomly stops, making what should be a fun moment feel more like a chore.

Overall, To the Moon is definitely worth playing if you’re in it for the story. I’d give it a 7/10—it could’ve been higher if not for the poor controls that chipped away at the experience.

I just finished To the Moon, and wow… I don’t think I was ready for this. My eyes are still wet, and my heart feels both heavy and warm at the same time. It’s not the kind of game you “play” in the traditional sense—it’s the kind you live through, quietly, almost like reading a book or watching a memory unfold. And then suddenly, you’re crying because it hit you in a place you didn’t expect.
River… oh, River. What an unforgettable character. She’s not loud, she’s not dramatic—she’s gentle, quiet, and impossibly human. The way her love and struggles are revealed piece by piece is so beautifully done that by the end, I just sat there thinking about her long after the game was over. She doesn’t just feel like a character; she feels like someone you once knew, someone you wish you could hug.
The story itself is simple yet devastatingly powerful. It talks about love, memory, regret, and the things we hold on to even when words fail us. And every moment is carried by that incredible soundtrack—those piano notes will stay with me forever.
It’s rare for a game to make me cry like this, but even rarer for it to leave me feeling grateful afterward. To the Moon is not about action or puzzles—it’s about empathy. About understanding someone’s heart, even when it’s complicated, even when it hurts.
If you’ve ever wondered whether a video game can make you feel something truly profound… play To the Moon. Just make sure you’ve got tissues nearby, and maybe someone to talk to when it’s over.

For as deep a discount as this game goes for a 3 to 4 hour story that tells a unique narrative that’s very likely to get a strong emotional response out of you, I think it’s very much worth the money. 

However, I recommend it with the caveat that you should please give the game some patience to properly get started. The first 30 to 45 minutes serve as a prologue before the narrative begins proper, and during this time the game is at its weakest in my opinion. 

Specifically, the game is setting up for an emotional narrative journey, and that’s what you expect from it when you buy it, but the first 30 to 45 minutes are spent with what is essentially a slapstick comedy duo slinging quips at each other with gags and language that make it hard to respect either of them as professional, rational adults, seeing as one of them says things like bro and epic even though he’s in his probably late 20s, and the other one says euphemisms for cursing that are awkward and unnatural, like what the potato. 

Once they start talking less and the characters the story is actually focusing on take the forefront, the  story becomes much more compelling in my opinion. So please don’t drop it 30 minutes in thinking the rest of the game will be like that, because it won’t be. And you’ll be missing out on a great story if you do.

The work of Kan exhibits many shared features. His games are like the early spring, when the snow melts halfway, white water flows, sunlight covers the ground, yet life has not quite awakened. We can hear the footsteps of spring, though its face remains indistinct.

The feeling of early spring is everywhere in his creations. The music, whether For River or Time Is a Place, is always gentle, warm, and tinged with solitude. The nostalgic pixel art evokes memory and intimacy. The story unfolds naturally from a calm surface. His sincerity flows like a small stream, melting slowly from the long winter.

The coldness comes from loneliness. Perhaps drawn from Kan’s own experience, his works always carry a trace of solitude. Dr. Rosalene has only Dr. Watts as her companion. The protagonists are often people near the end of their lives, for whom loneliness seems fated. Even when friends and family surround them, their inner sorrows remain unspoken, locked behind walls of the heart. Only at the final moment, through the winding reconstruction of memory by Sigmund Corp (perhaps inspired by Sigmund Freud?), can the truth finally be unearthed.

The way out of loneliness is through genuine feeling. Even when unspoken or unseen, Kan’s characters possess rich inner worlds. John carries within him River and Joey; Colin carries Faye, his wife Sofia, and his family. They find peace in life precisely because they are, at heart, warm and delicate souls. I believe that even without Sigmund Corp, if they quietly revisited their memories, they would still discover that their lives were, in their own way, happy.

Memory threads together the fragments of a story, and these fragments form the present self. If something had been done differently at the beginning, everything that followed might also have changed. Thinking this way, the world becomes countless parallel timelines running side by side. Yet no matter which timeline one inhabits, a person remains the same, and the noise and fury, the sorrow and bliss, remain unchanged. John, whether or not he meets River, will always find her on the moon. And in that final world without sorrow or darkness, they shall still be together.

Even after leaving this world, their warmth lingers. John leaves his fortune to the caretaker; Colin has a happy family. The authentic feeling born of solitude announces the coming of spring. That river runs into the story that continues beyond, through years, and many years later.

To the Moon is a unique experience in videogames. Featuring a top-down, 16 bit graphical style with simple gameplay and puzzles, the game delves into powerful themes like love, loss, mortality, and human connection. We follow the story of Johnny, an older terminally-ill man, who's life wish was to travel to the moon. We play as two doctors hired to enter his mind and alter his memories; beginning with his childhood and moving along throughout his life. Along the way they discover his hopes, dreams, as well as fears and regrets until reaching a gut-wrenching finale. It is a short but profound narrative, and one that really hits you in the feels.

It is a touching science-fiction drama about true love, loss, family, following your heart, and fulfilling someone's seemingly impossible dying wish. What I did forget, however, is the ending and how it will leave you questioning your own deepest desires and life choices. Overall, it is an unexpectedly striking and creative game at its core that will undoubtedly leave you an emotional wreck if you can look past the negatives I have mentioned. [h2]Short Summary[/h2]

[b]To The Moon[/b] is not a game you play; it is a story you feel. This four-hour journey into a dying man's memories is an emotional masterpiece that will break your heart and put it back together.

[h2]The Breakdown[/h2]

[table]
[tr]
[td][h3]What We Loved[/h3][/td]
[td]The reverse-chronological storytelling creates a compelling mystery. The masterful original score defines the emotional peaks. It handles themes of love, regret, and neurodivergence with unmatched grace.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Minor Annoyances[/h3][/td]
[td]The actual gameplay is minimal and often feels like an interruption. The puzzles are trivial roadblocks. The RPG Maker engine imposes strict visual limitations on the presentation.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]What It's About[/h3][/td]
[td]Two doctors traverse a dying man's memories to fulfill his final wish. It explores the persistence of love and the difficult task of reconciling with a life full of regrets.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]How It Plays[/h3][/td]
[td]You search for mementos to unlock memory links. The gameplay acts as a pacing mechanism and a vehicle for the music rather than a challenge. It grounds the story in tangible objects.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Core Tone[/h3][/td]
[td]Bittersweet melancholy mixes with whimsical humor. The atmosphere is quiet and introspective, building toward a tragic yet beautiful resolution.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Genre Context[/h3][/td]
[td]A narrative adventure similar to [b]Finding Paradise[/b] or [b]Rakuen[/b]. It strips away the combat of classic JRPGs to focus entirely on the story.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][h3]Technical Snapshot[/h3][/td]
[td]The evocative 16-bit pixel art is charming but basic. The piano soundtrack is the technical highlight and carries the experience. The engine is functional but dated.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h2]The Bottom Line[/h2]

[h3]Who Is This For?[/h3]
Players who value emotional storytelling and incredible music above all else, and are willing to read a visual novel disguised as an RPG.

[h3]Who Is This Not For?[/h3]
Gamers seeking challenging mechanics, complex puzzles, or high-fidelity graphics who will be bored by the lack of interactivity.

[quote]Prepare tissues, because this short narrative payload delivers one of the most poignant love stories in the medium.[/quote]

[h2]Main Review[/h2]

You play as Dr. Watts and Dr. Rosalene, memory architects hired to fulfill the dying wish of Johnny Wyles. His request is simple but inexplicable: he wants to go to the moon. Your role shifts between objective observers and emotional detectives. You do not fight enemies. You dive into Johnny's mind to rewrite his past. The central conflict is internal. You must uncover why he wants this specific wish before his heart stops.

The gameplay experience is strictly defined by narrative discovery. You traverse memories in reverse, moving from old age back to childhood. The interaction loop involves light exploration to find mementos and solving simple tile-flipping puzzles to break memory barriers. These mechanics serve as contextual anchors. They force you to pay attention to the environment but offer no real challenge. The gameplay exists solely to pace the dialogue and give the soundtrack room to breathe.

The world of [b]To The Moon[/b] is small but emotionally dense. The aesthetic relies on evocative 16-bit pixel art that leaves room for imagination. However, the atmosphere is defined by Kan Gao’s score. The piano melodies dictate the emotional stakes more than the dialogue. The pacing is a slow-burn mystery. It starts with whimsical banter between the doctors and slowly descends into a heartbreaking study of neurodivergence and connection. The reverse chronology turns the story into a jigsaw puzzle that you solve piece by piece.

The value here lies entirely in the narrative payload. It is a short, impactful journey that respects your time. While the visual limitations of the engine are obvious and the interactivity is nearly non-existent, the writing transcends these flaws. The portrayal of a relationship strained by unspoken conditions is nuanced and mature. If you approach this as a linear visual novel, it is flawless. If you expect a game, you will be disappointed.

This late diagnosis has left quite a few scars on my development, and this aspect is also emphasised in this game. 

Apart from Josh from Watch Dogs 2, I've never seen another character in a video game who is meant to be on the spectrum. That was very nice to see and aside from that, the story as a whole is very good and touching. The music and world design really enhance the atmosphere. There are also quite a lot of funny moments. Only downside is that you have to control your character by clicking with your mouse for 95% of the game but for whatever reason, you can finally move around with arrow keys in the last 20 minutes - this should've been a thing from the very beginning. I can’t believe I’ve never written a review for this game after all these years. I’ve played countless JRPGs and MMOs over the decades, but this little gem remains my favorite video game of all time.

It was originally gifted to me by my ex-boyfriend. As a huge Cloud and Tifa shipper from the OG Final Fantasy VII, he thought I’d fall in love with Johnny and River’s story: two childhood sweethearts bound by memories, loss, and love.

Johnny and River’s journey is a powerful reminder to cherish the ones we love while facing the memories we often bury. It also shines a compassionate light on neurodivergence and the barriers it can create in understanding and connection. Everything about this story from the writing, the pacing, the emotions is breathtaking, compelling, and absolutely award-worthy.

The music, though, is what truly elevates it. When my beloved dog passed away, this soundtrack was playing softly in the background.

Even as I write this, I’m crying. The themes of memory, love, and letting go feel more relevant than ever as we inch closer to the kind of technology this game imagined ; technology that might one day let us revisit our most precious memories in our final moments or achieve the dreams we couldn't reach during our gifted time.

The creator deserves recognition as one of the most emotionally intelligent storytellers of our time.

[h2]I loved this game, but not it's representation[/h2]

I'll start this off by saying I'm autistic, most my family is, I went to a school for people who are, so when I talk about the autism representation don't think I'm just some moral elitist trying to exercise my moral superiority, but I'll get to that later.

I loved this game, it's sweet, it manages dialogue properly, instead of just endless text boxes and exposition all the dialogue serves a purpose, and you actually want to read it, it really feels like different people interacting, with their own lives, personalities, experiences, everything. I'm not into reading, I struggle to pay attention and retain what I read, I'd like to be able to enjoy reading, there's books I'd love to be able to read, but unfortunately it just doesn't work for me, and dyslexia is doing me no favours, but this game's text is absolutely masterful, it's accessible and actually immersive, you want to read it all regardless if you enjoy reading, there was no point I decided to skim anything except for the 3 books in the real world, and even those I went back to with a new perspective later in the game.

There are so many subtle moments in this game which give you the opportunity to see things in a different light, but also don't think it's just completely emotion based and has no substance beyond that, it's funny, it's packed with little references and I'm sure you'll probably appreciate at least 1 in your playthrough, and the tile flipping gameplay was simple but fun, although I do have to criticise it for not allowing you to reset it from within the game and try to get the minimum moves, it's not tough, but it's still fun, it's accessible enough that you can figure out it, but enough to keep you interested in doing well, although the tiles flipping does seem a bit buggy when you try to do multiple at once, so be patient with that.

The story is pretty great, going through the memories of someone dying to try and give them a better end, and then considering "is this the right thing to do? Would they really want this if they knew the full extent of what it would be?" it really encourages some deeper philosophical considerations about reality, and I appreciate the inclusion of subtle references to laws which could arise as a result of this technology, and I appreciate the fact you're a team of 2 doing this, it keeps things from getting stale or going by too fast, having these characters that can bounce off of each other or have little moments of conflict.

I have a couple points of contention with some aspects of the story, I think the inclusion of Joey could be a point of debate, but there's not anything specific where I think "this should absolutely have been removed" or "why include this?" Nothing is completely and totally unreasonable, although the [spoiler]medication affecting his memory[/spoiler] can get a little close for some I'm sure, I don't think I'd necessarily change anything about the story though, I think it's all fine as it is despite the criticisms I've got coming, I think it's great, the soundtrack is amazing, at first glance the pixel art may seem very typical RPG maker in style but it's got some little aspects to it which make it distinct, which I appreciate so much as a pixel artist.

But now for my criticisms of the representation, spoilers ahead: I don't completely hate it, I just think it could've been better, and in some ways it serves to drag characters down, John treats it like a big deal getting the diagnosis and it just makes you go "what? Nothing's changed, what's the big deal?" No one needs fixing, the horse therapy I was like "okay it worked for her which was very sweet but that's not how it is for most people", how is equine therapy the first thing suggested? Why was anything even suggested? What was the problem? They love each other right? And then he doesn't want to read the book about autism? Why? Dude you love her and you won't even put the effort into understanding her better? But also, she's not great representation either.

I at least appreciate that it's pointed out how even for someone who's autistic, the repeatedly making paper bunnies is still not quite typical, but the way Isabelle acts about her getting diagnosed like "I envy her, she's free", being diagnosed young or not doesn't make a difference how well you do integrating into society, it's an explanation for things you may not understand about yourself, it's a way you can hopefully get the accommodations you need (which really should be available to everyone regardless), it can help if you're struggling with something, to know how you may react differently, or what may help, but I hate how dramatised it is, being autistic is not a big deal and I hate that it's kind of painted as one, I don't think it ruined anything for me, but it did get on my nerves.

I'm fine with her being less social, although I hate that she's treated as socially inept as she is though, because it's over-dramatic, it's a poor characterisation of autism, but at least they say "everyone with it is different" although in all honesty, instead of "with it" I wish they said "like it", because I'm not with autism, I don't have autism, I am autistic, I am different from neurotypicals because I am autistic, it's not a separate entity from me or anything that could be removed although some may try (hey btw don't try to cure autism I deserve to exist as much as anyone), it's just part of me.

Enough of that though, if that put you off, trust me, it's not as bad as I make it sound, this game is still phenomenal and I still think you should play it, if there was anything I'd do differently though, it'd be the way autism is represented, specifically how dramatic it is, moving on though, the ending, I thought it was fairly fitting, it was bittersweet, but if it's between him going to the moon and never seeing her again, or a compromise between that and his original memories, I'll absolutely take this, I don't think he needed to go to the moon though, we don't even see him on the moon, because it was never being there that mattered, I think you can interpret him wanting to go to the moon as him wanting to have understood River better, (although I'd like that interpretation a little more if he didn't say he'd rather not read the fucking book about autism?) but however you interpret it, I think it's still incredibly sweet.

I loved this game so much, despite my hangup about the autism representation, and I'd absolutely recommend this, especially if you're a fan of emotional storytelling, good soundtracks, or RPG maker games, give this a go, it's fairly linear, but not in a way that feels restrictive, you're on rails but for the most part you don't see the rails, because you're invested in the story and the characters and seeing the best for everyone.

Before I end this off though, I do want to add 1 thing... I don't get the inclusion of the heart rate monitor... Maybe it's an immersion thing? I don't know, I just thought "well I can only ever see it on the pause menu and I have to wait to even see any bumps, what's the point of this?" I expected it to be more integrated into the gameplay or immersion in some way, do something and see it in the corner affecting his heartrate, but I get it, it wouldn't quite make sense, still, I don't really get it's inclusion, maybe it was as an explanation for being able to hear the heart monitor at times, but they're in the room with the one that's actually hooked up to him so they could just hear it and it manifests in there, small gripe, doesn't really impact anything, just something I noticed.

If you haven't played this game, play it, maybe get it on sale if you're hesitant about getting a game that's so linear or doesn't have a ton of replay value, but absolutely give it a go, I'm definitely going to be trying to other games in the series.

[h1]I came for the soundtrack, and I leave with a hole in my heart.[/h1]

This game came to me [strikethrough]in a dream[/strikethrough] years ago when I saw Markiplier and the likes played it for the first time. Granted, I never watched those videos but soundtracks and covers made it to me and that was my first exposure to the game. I've learned [b]Everything's Alright – Laura Shigihara[/b] on the acoustic guitar first before I even had the chance to play the game. It was such a powerful song in it's own that even now, years have passed, I can still play it on the guitar. That's just how impactful this game was, and we're only talking about the soundtrack yet.

[h2]What is the weight of one's dreams?[/h2]
It's hard to give a justified review of this game without spoiling it [i](but then again, it's been more than a decade so the statue of limitations for spoilers must have passed by now)[/i]. The story this game gives is nothing short of phenomenal. From Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts' natural back and forth banters, all the way through the crux of why they do the things they do. This story tugs your heartstrings as you venture deeper into the story, and the pay-off in the end of it all is what brings everything together. The game follows a non-linear storyline as you go through and sift through the numerous memories of a dying man, finding the reason for his dreams. There's a lot of classic twists and gags you'd enjoy, some outdated, and some managed to still hit despite the time gap from the release. Honestly, if you want to know more, you'd actually have to play the game because I for one, am not spoiling it this time.

[h2]It is definitely a product of its time.[/h2]
And by that, I'm referring to the game's graphic and controls. This game was made way back in 2011, so comparing it to new games, it's not fair. It's a very rigid control system, especially on turning corners and seemingly invisible walls. But that doesn't really matter much since most of the time it's clear and concise where the game wants you to go and where things should be. Despite those obstacles, even if you play it now, the characters in this game are still very expressive thanks to emotive sprites and animated movement (as much as a pixel art can move) that conveys every character present in the scene as [i]alive[/i]. 

[h2]My ears are in heaven.[/h2]
The OST for this game is absolutely perfect. Kan Gao and Laura Shigihara [spoiler][i](our beloved PvZ composer and vocalist, and Rakuen creator)[/i][/spoiler] did such an amazing job on this game. There was never a dull moment in the game, whether you were wandering around to find stuff or just listening to the "For River" piano in the mansion; the music from this game breathed in so much life into the story.

[h2]And to the moon we go. See you there.[/h2]
And where does that bring us? Well, to the moon, no doubt. It's grown to be one of my favorite story games I've ever played throughout the years. I've played this on and off every now and then since it's a short story (somehow didn't record offline playing back then for some reason) and I really wanted to put my review out there despite it being long overdue [i]by a few years[/i]. I'm still gathering the time and courage to play the sequels and other games released the same studio. Regardless, if you do buy this, make sure you have tissues on hand. [b]TO THE MOON gets a 9/10 from me.[/b]

Here is my review for To the Moon:

First off, gameplay is basic and standard RPG maker. You walk around and press the button to interact. That's it. You don't do any fighting (but there was a joke of a fight at the start of the game). And you are usually locked within a room or two with one or two interactive items. Ironically, gameplay is not the focus of this game.

Story, that's what this game is all about. It could have simply been a story or a visual novel and the experience would've likely been the same. You play as two scientists who assist dying old folks. These elderly have regrets from their life and you provide them with solace. You do so by jumping into their memories and seeing them play through. An aged old man was once a middle aged man living his life, who was once a spry young lad with a glimmer of hope in his eyes. You then rewrite those memories to rewrite the future. Of course, this is all in the dying person's head, but their last experiences will be that of achieving their goals and finding peace. In this case you are helping an old man reach the moon. It tells the story of his life, his wife, disease, and past trauma. I won't go too much into it, as that would take too long. The game also includes DLC mini-episodes about the two scientists you play as well as their science company. This also sets up the sequels. 期待值过高，其实整体而言形式和故事都还不错，但就是确实结尾有点弱下去了，把整个体验感都打散了。
整个故事最touch的点其实是当所有人都以为river精神失常，并且患有疾病，是john一直在包容、解释、做出努力时，作者给出一记重锤，告诉观者，其实river才是那个清晰地记得一切，并始终如一守候在被抹去记忆的john身边的人，她所有看似反常的举动，都是竭尽全力用自己的方式想要唤醒john。而john尽管失去了重要的记忆，也在一次又一次选择中选择着、爱着river。
这个“皆大欢喜”的双赢结局没有问题，但遗憾的点就在于，在这份虚假的欢喜之后，没有把故事再重新拉回来，拉回这两个真正的人身上，反而给出长达1-5分钟的体量去描绘飞船升空的过程，这并不是任何人真正的意图，故事中除了作者给出的强设定：“不让john在记忆的物理层面上去月球，俩博士就得上法庭”以外，没有人在意john会不会真的在物理层面上去到月球。
动机是爱，是情感，是john在千千万万次遗忘过后依旧挂念的、没由来的、根植在潜意识中的对river的爱，是孩提懵懂无知时许下的天真诺言。这哪里需要真的在物理层面实现，并且这一类的经历观众也并不想看到这个物理层面如同现实世界一般的、逻辑链严谨的“结局”。
把双胞胎救回来，“移除”river的设置也很诡异，台词给出的触动点是“没关系他会找到另一个river”，突然搞出替身文学。在玩家（观者）几乎完全沉浸在john和river的故事中后，直接换了个主角，强迫观者在几秒钟之内把情感瞬间挪移到另一个故事里去，太奇怪了。但是john有个双胞胎这个设置作为悬疑的炸点很牛逼，起一身鸡皮疙瘩。
总的来说john的故事有三条主要情感（人生）线，一条是现实世界joey死去，一直在吃阻断药的john和river两人度过相爱、模糊却也苦涩的一生；一条是利用机器干涉后的世界，joey被复活，john和他的双胞胎兄弟过着相知相依的前半生，没有太大的波澜，并且双双获得超乎常人的成功；第三条是在nasa遇到river的虚假的后半生。
游戏百分之七八十的体量都给了前两条线，在这其中，john是立体的，现实世界的river是立体的，joey也是立体的。好，玩家接受了，进入了，结果突然在最后蹦出来虚假世界中的joey和river，并且还不加以刻画，导致他们仿佛凭空跳出来的两个扁平新人物，并以这二人和john作为最后的结尾？有种你为之付出了很多努力去让他寻找自我的人，突然跟两个莫名其妙蹦出来的陌生人跑到了一个你不相信也不太认可的世界里去了的感觉。把整个情感和故事线都给在最后关头打散了。

I've been trying to think of how to review To the Moon for several days now. Part of me wants to approach it chiefly as the vital piece of indie-game history that it represents. Another part wants to completely set that reputation aside and look it at as a game and narrative by itself. But I've struggled to make much progress through either angle, and part of why might be that I don't like To the Moon as much as I remember liking it.

To be clear, To the Moon is broadly successful and even more broadly a good game. It's plotted well, decently pretty, has a great soundtrack and is surprisingly good at tugging on the old heart strings. All that said though, it's still clearly the work of someone who is still far from mastering their craft.

Much of the dialogue is - for want of a better (or less online) word - cringe as hell. Most of the attempts at comedy fall pretty flat and leave To the Moon's tone feeling more uneven than it should. I'm all for levity in sad stories, but where the more emotional side of the storytelling has aged surprisingly gracefully, the comedy feels extremely 2011 in the worst way possible. It's not agonisingly bad, but there was more than a few eyeroll-inducing moments throughout its short runtime. And as well written as some of its more touching moments are, certain revelations feel more than a little rushed and a little contrived. There was obviously a strong desire to have big reveals and shocking twists and much of the story has been mangled around to better accomodate them, perhaps at the expense of the relatability that it could have had. Also, the slightly naff puzzles present only to fend off the early 2010s "not a game if no gameplay" crowd really don't need to be here and I'm glad they get dropped about two thirds of the way through.

As much as these flaws do work against the experience and prevent To the Moon from being a masterpiece, they do add a certain charm. Games like this aren't really made any more. You no longer have to manhandle a shitty engine like RPG Maker to make a touching, narrative-driven, no-combat game like this, you can just press a button on Gamemaker and it will all but generate one for you. While game development getting easier is great for accessibility, there is now a certain level of homogenisation in indie games as less sacrifices need to be made to accomodate certain limits. To the Moon works as a great time capsule for the early days of the indie boom, and I imagine I will return to it again someday not too far into the future. In part, I'm glad I wasn't so enamoured with it on this revisit, as it will make it easier to approach the two sequels that I've put off playing for so long. If you haven't played To the Moon, it's not the absolute, unrivalled must-play that it once was. But it is an excellent time capsule and will probably get a good few tears out of you by the end of its four hour playtime.

To the moon is a point & click/interactive visual novel in which you play as two scientists, who visit a dying man. Your task is to fulfill his last wish: to go to the moon. But to do this, you need to find out what made him want this. You essentially experience his life backwards from a third person perspective. The game play isn't challenging at all, as it's fully a story-driven game. The plot and the music are the main attractions that'll stay with you for years after you finish the game. The sequels are good, too, albeit IMO not quite as good as the original.

You explore places to find various clues or items that help you learn more about the story, and talk to or watch interactions between characters. There are also recurring puzzle mini games, though those are not meant to be the main focus— they mainly just give you breaks from the story to think about what has happened and try to piece together answers. Additionally, the games can also derail into other “joke” mini games (like trying to do a turn-based-rpg fight against a squirrel, or something equally silly). There is only one instance of ‘silly mini-games’ in the series in which your success or failure substantially influences the direction of the story; even for that one, failing it doesn’t give you a ‘bad ending’.

As for the writing, one of the game's main themes is asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism and how it affects personal relationships. That's a pretty unique premise for a video game and it does a great job conveying the emotions involves. A lot of western media just portrays AS as being an emotionless robot which is a wildly ignorant and outdated take. This game might not get it perfect, but it does a way better job than most of the representation out there. When people are praising games like Beyond Eyes for representation, the bar is pretty low.

One thing that stuck with me years after playing To The Moon was how bittersweet its ending was. It didn't sugarcoat how unambiguously sad were the lives that some of the cast got to experience. This game was not about the moment-by-moment, action-packed gameplay, but rather a slow, methodical journey showing how someone's past affects their state of mind. The main take away for me was about the incredible value that love injects into our lives. It was a game that surprised the player by having a compelling story rise above a standard RPGMaker elements; the simple graphics and twee dialog.

I think what made it work is how silly the game was in the majority of the story. Stuff like the main characters Dr. Rosalene using random vegetables as curse words and Dr. Watts shouting random pop-culture references from Dragon Ball Z and Hulk to hype himself up. Genuinely made me laugh a good amount despite the feels. It's the opposite of brilliant banter, but its very idiocy hit home for me. Because most people devolve approximately to this level of stupidity when they're letting their guard down with a friend. It's human nature to be stupid when you're trying to recover emotional energy: smartness takes a lot of effort. If you keep trying to find the smartest thing you could do when you're chilling out, then your "chilling out" isn't going to be very restful.

To The Moon is a bit like the Shoebox Project in this manner: it's cringeworthy in its stupidity, but adorable in how close it is to real communication between actual humans. Leave brilliant banter for pirate adventures and other works of deliberately unrealistic human interaction. This is slice-of-life. It has different literary standards. The game came out in 2011 anyhow, when that kind of random speech was at peak popularity in nerd subcultures. People may feel a certain way about the writing and the jokes, and I get that. Some of the humour didn’t age well. However, when the story hits a beat, it hit HARD for me. I remember going through dialogue between Rosalene and Watts during one of the big story beats, and just hitting this realization that explained the title of the game and reframed the whole story. Threw me for a loop.

If you’re looking for gameplay, this isn’t it. However, if you want an incredible story, then you found the first in a perfect series. It’s one of those games where you have to take the entire package into consideration when reviewing it. If you look at all the individual aspects of the game, it's kind of average/okay. But where it really shines is with its emotional impact. I highly recommend To the Moon. The story hit me really hard, and I hope I can get some more people to experience it.

To The Moon, developed using RPG Maker, may not boast cutting edge graphics or elaborate gameplay mechanics, but it delivers something far more enduring: a deeply emotional narrative interwoven with philosophical depth and introspective storytelling.

The game follows two doctors, Neil Watts and Eva Rosalene, who work for a company that grants dying patients their last wish by altering their memories. Their latest client, an elderly man named John, wishes to go to the moon but doesn't know why. The story unfolds as Neil and Eva dive into his memories, moving backwards through his life to uncover the origin of his mysterious desire.

What makes this narrative structure so captivating is its meta layer: we, as players, are essentially watching two characters experience a man's life as if viewing a film. Their commentary serves as both comic relief and philosophical reflection, drawing us deeper into the story. It feels almost like watching your favorite Twitch streamer or YouTuber play through a game except here, the game is someone's life, and the stakes are heartbreakingly real. (But imagine watching your favorite Youtuber or Twitch Streamer playing the game and controlling Neil and Eva who are watching Johns Memories through the Memory Machine. So many layers)

The emotional impact is heightened by the game's masterful duality between romance and realism which is a reccuring theme in the game. At the heart of the narrative is the complex relationship between John and his wife River. These two characters embody the game's central philosophical theme:

John, the dreamer, represents romanticism. His longing to "go to the moon" is not just a literal wish, but a symbol of his search for purpose and transcendence. He's driven by emotion, nostalgia, and the yearning to rewrite a life filled with missed connections and unanswered questions.

River, by contrast, is the anchor of realism. Her actions often seem puzzling or emotionally distant, yet they're grounded in quiet intention and a deep, unspoken understanding of life's limitations. She clings to truth, even when it's painful. Her struggle with her autism spectrum disorder is portrayed with subtlety and respect. River doesn't seek to reshape the past or escape into fantasy; instead, she holds fiercely to moments of sincerity and authenticity.

Their relationship is where the emotional weight of the game truly lies. John wants to change the past so that he can find a sense of fulfillment, but River quietly accepts the imperfect present. This conflict becomes a lens through which the game explores profound philosophical questions: Is it better to remember a comforting lie or a painful truth? Can a rewritten memory give life meaning or does meaning come from how we face reality?

Despite its many strengths, To The Moon is not without flaws. The story, while moving, can at times feel overly sentimental or emotionally manipulative, leaning heavily on tragic tropes to evoke a response. Some plot points especially involving River's condition and John's childhood could have been explored with greater depth and nuance. Additionally, the setting, though charming in its pixel art simplicity, sometimes feels too static or sparse, which can make the world feel a bit underdeveloped compared to the emotional weight it carries. Some of the situations between Eva and Neil can be a little cringeworthy, but at least they break up the serious tone from time to time.

And of course there are also the logical questions that naturally wonder whether it wouldn't somehow be illegal to access the memories of others due to data protection laws or human rights and why a company would specialize in this and conduct research without thoroughly protecting itself from the law and consequences. Yes, there's certainly something to that, but this is a romanticized story and not everything has to make sense. Deal with it, you realist.

That said, these shortcomings are relatively minor when weighed against the game's overall achievement. To The Moon may be humble in presentation, but it reaches emotional heights few big budget titles dare to attempt. It's not just a story about a man who wants to go to the moon, it's a meditation on love, memory, regret, and the quiet power of a life lived.

To The Moon's core concept, a dying man trying to fulfill a final wish through memory-based technology, is simultaneously compelling from a science fiction perspective, and deeply sad. I bought the game because it was well reviewed, and because that concept intrigued me. However I found myself unable to finish it due to several key frustrations.

Chief among these is the game's uneven tone. The game's writing constantly alternates between inappropriate or ill-conceived humor, and scenes that are supposed to tug at your heartstrings in a frankly very sappy manner. But that sappiness is what we're playing for, and buying into, so it's very disconcerting to have so many flat attempts at humorous asides completely break the mood. While there were some charming moments that made me laugh, and I certainly appreciate the proper and necessary usage of comic relief, the game's designers took it several steps too far. Furthermore, the game's retro art style and JRPG interface really limits the emotional impact of the narrative, and doesn't really bring anything to the table on it's own.

One particularly frustrating aspect of this is the asinine gameplay, involving fetch quests, idiotic "memory-breaking" activities, and totally inappropriate JRPG-style fight scenes. What little gameplay is present is not really very enjoyable. It's enough to make one question whether this story would be better told in a different medium. Dear Esther, another game that was very short, focused on narrative, and had minimal gameplay, at least existed in a 3D engine and had some really beautiful visuals. Dear Esther also didn't force you to play silly minigames in order to advance the narrative.

A bright spot in To The Moon is the soundtrack, which, if you're in the mood for sentimentality, really hits the spot. However it's better enjoyed without the game getting in the way. To be honest, I would recommend that people simply watch an LP of the game rather than play it, and skip over the "gamey" sequences. Or just read a plot summary while listening to the soundtrack, and maybe look up a couple of key sequences on YouTube. Either option would be far less frustrating than actually playing the game.

[h1] A Review More entertaining than the game it talks about [/h1] 
[h3] Guaranteed to make you laugh [/h3]

Let me begin by saying I haven't finished the game at the time of writing this review, i couldn't.  I'd like to give this game a rating between thumbs up and thumbs down... perhaps a middle finger!

First things first, I totally understand wanting to respect the bandwagon... yes, tons of reviews have given this a thumbs up, and the number of thumbs down are negligible... but i can't do that. Why?

In this case, the reviews are entirely disconnected from the actual experience the game affords. Reviews present a prospective buyer with an expectation of what the experience will be like. Everyone is different, what you like may not be what I like, but I read reviews in that light, and understand there will be differences. If you tell me you loved an experience and why, I believe you and translate that into a portrait of ideas of how the game will be. If that portrait seems like it will be something that fits my likes, then I will give the game a try. In most games, you can average a bunch of reviews, pros and cons, and arrive at a general expectation of experience, but occasionally a game has a lot of misleading reviews. I think that is the case for this game. Let me elaborate.

A lot of reviews read the same:
* outstanding story
* makes you cry
* phenomenal soundtrack
* fantastic pixel art
! Yada yada...

No. Just, NO!... No on every count. 

Don't get me wrong, the music is not terrible, it can even be good. Even, dare I say, above par. But it's not phenomenal, it doesn't even rank top 40%.  it's really rather depressing, actually. 

Pixel Art? Nope. I wouldn't call this art. I've seen a ton of pixel art games, and this one falls short on so many levels. It's not just that the art is bad, or not good, it doesn't capture that special magic or mystique that makes pixel art so beloved. There's nothing special about this game in that department. A lot of stuff is really hard to distinguish what you're looking at, and nothing really stands out as great... nothing gives you that sit back and say "ahh" feeling.

Right about now someone is reading this and saying, "OK, fair enough. But I know what you're gonna say next and don't you dare say the story isn't the Crème de la Crème!".  Sorry, but this disjointed mess of a story with nonsensical dialog that adds nothing to a narrative or the characters, along with the very dry humor that makes regular dry humor seem funny, is nothing to write home about... Maybe, complain about. 

The characters are uninteresting, the total lack of backstory before delving into the experience is unforgivable, and 1.6 hours into playing this game I've not experienced anything that makes me want to continue playing it except to try to get something for my money. This is really boring, and I hate to say that, but it's true. The dialog constantly left me more irritated than if nothing was said at all, and the characters became less interesting with every jump back in time I took. That's really saying something when you begin with no interest.  Please, do not pretend this story makes you care about the characters, it's just embarrassing at this point.

I think the single most proliferated point in the reviews was that this game will make you cry. This is also probably the most outrageous lie about the game. To make one cry, one must be invested emotionally. This game couldn't even make me remotely care about any of the uninteresting and bad-dialogued characters, how the hell will it make me cry? The tragedy is revealed in the beginning, before you know anything about the characters. The woman died... OK, everyone dies eventually. The woman is crazy, fine. Lots of people are off their rockers, just turn on the TV and watch for five minutes. None of these things are spoilers, they are among the first things you are presented with in the game. 

The story utterly failed to build any interest in it or the characters more than an hour and a half into this purely story-driven narrative. If this was a game where you went out exploring, farming and building in-between story segments, that statement would have little meaning. But this game is pure story, and your exploration is limited to point-click from an inch away from the last story advancement in a game that probably only has a couple hours of total game-play in it.  In other words, 1.6 hours of pure story is equivalent to several days or weeks of playing in a lot of other games. And in all this time, having followed the story into introduction and exploration of main characters, I've seen nothing to even remotely make me interested in them. 

There isn't one thing that even makes me want to keep playing just to find out what it turns out to be or how it ends. And why would that make me cry? Heck, I even consider myself an emotionally sensitive person with empathetic imagination, it wouldn't take much to get me to build up something to cry over in an ankle-deep drama.

I guess for those easily influenced by depressing music there may be some cry-factor here. If you have personal, real-life tragedies that vaguely connect to the disjointed and shallow ideas presented in-between the nonsensical dialog then maybe you can cry because it reminds you of those. 

Yes, it almost seems like the developer was trying to make this game meaningful, but it's virtues in that regard were built up in me by reading a crap-ton of reviews that set the stage for that expectation. Had I played this game without reading any reviews or information about it, I'd have stopped playing within a few minutes and never gone back to this waste of time. The only thing memorable about this game is the total scam the reviews amount to. I'll always remember how thousands of (likely paid shill) reviews propped this game up on a pedestal when it belongs in a pit under an outhouse.

I'm totally not being unfair. This is supported by the fact the numerous "good" reviews utterly fail to give a valid reason for this game being good. Most of them are a few lines that read like hype. "THIS IS A GOOD 'UN", or "MADE ME CRY, WILL MAKE YOU CRY TOO!". They aren't detailing the reason WHY the game is good. They are merely telling you it's good. That is opinion, and not even opinion supported by facts and reason. That is hype. Telling you to buy a game 'cuz it will make you cry is not a reason to buy a game. If it really did invest you emotionally, and such recommendations were accurate, then one can decide if emotional games are a value they find worth paying for. 

I guess i've learned a lesson here. I should've done more research. Perhaps spoiled the chance that the game's experience was good by watching actual game-play videos on Youtube or something. I bought the hype, and I got what I payed for before playing the game. I bought hype, I got hype. The game was just the cardboard below the cake. It may not taste good, but it will forever remind me of the hype I purchased, and occasionally, if I close my eyes real tight and imagine real hard, I can lick that cake board and pretend I'm tasting the hype cake again.

I have seen a lot of praise for the story for To The Moon. This is one time where the praise was due. What I saw of the story was very well done. The problem I had was that most everything else, aside from an awesome soundtrack, was not. Had this been a kinetic visual novel I would have enjoyed it much more. Had it had better thought out puzzles, such as Rakuen, I would have enjoyed it much more. Sadly what I was left with was a quality story that to enjoy I had to wade through input issues; low frame rates; and poor puzzles. The input issues were such that when I clicked on a location for my character to move they sometimes would go there. Other times they would go part way and stop. The same would happen when I clicked on objects to investigate, sometimes they would go right to it and others only a bit and stop. The puzzles mostly consisted of mini games of “preparing” mementos to go further back in Johnny’s memories. To do this you had to clear away white blocks on a picture by pressing buttons that correspond to columns and rows. In doing so you would creat white blocks elsewhere. You had to anticipate where they would form (there is a pattern) and you could them clear them all. I found this pretty annoying. Even the basic puzzles of finding keys had issues at times. I was supposed to read this passage of a book to find a key hidden there but it wasn’t until the third time I read the passage that my character found the key.

	I played To The Moon on Linux. It never crashed on me once. There are no graphics options at all. Alt-Tab doesn’t work. It uses a total of 223MB of disk space. It uses the RPG Maker XP engine. The game allows you to manually save at any time outside of dialogue and has 3 save slots. There is also an auto save feature for those who prefer that. During play my GPU usage was 3-7%; my VRAM usage was 537-594MB; my CPU usage was 0-3%; my RAM usage was 2.6-3GB and my frame rate was a constant 40 FPS. Why it was stuck at 40 I have no idea.

Your enjoyment of the game will hinge on whether you value story and whether you have similar pet peaves as me with gameplay.

[u]In short:[/u] To the Moon is a flawed narrative with a few (rather badly executed) game elements tacked on. I appreciate some interesting concepts and themes, but there are also some glaring problems with the writing. The soundtrack is very good, but did not compensate for my general frustration with the game. Even for 3.5 hours of playtime (and some free DLC on top) the full asking-price strikes me as ridiculous, but at least the sale and bundle discounts are substantial.

[u]In long:[/u] This is a game made in RPG Maker. [b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b] mainly consists in advancing dialogue prompts. Every few minutes you have to explore a restricted area and find 5 clues, followed by a miniscule tile-flipping puzzle. The exploration parts handle badly. Movement seems to be tile based and is only possible laterally (not diagonally). I found myself constantly getting hung up on various objects and characters as it is often entirely unclear which areas are traversible (invisible walls, some flowers cannot be stepped on while others can, some characters block while others are ghosts, etc). There is no indication which objects (clues) are interactable, so you'll end up pressing your character against every surface in hopes that something might happen. About half-way through the game this mechanic is phased out and other, strange and very jarring gameplay segments are tacked on (horse riding, whack-a-mole, action segment with dodging and shooting, even a real-world trivia question with its own ugly interface to enter an answer).

In terms of [b][u]technical aspects[/u][/b] the situation is equally dire. The game starts in full-screen and has zero options. No volume control, no resolution control, no built-in windowed mode (Alt-Enter puts the game in a tiny fixed-resolution window). It messes with your mouse sensitivity, to the point where I found it only playable with keyboard. The main mechanic is going through dialogue and for the most part one click/press fills out the current box and the second advances to the next text box. Towards the end this just flat-out stops working for about 20 minutes, forcing you to sit through the text slowly appearing, even if you could read a lot faster. There were no game-breaking bugs or crashes, but it's just made very cheaply and sloppily.

Alright, let's be honest, nobody's playing this for the amazing gameplay, so let's finally delve into the [b][u]writing[/u][/b] and start with the [u]good parts[/u]: The basic premise is already in the marketing material - You're travelling backwards through a dying man's memories to figure out how to implant a faux memory of him getting to the moon. The concept of gradually revealing what made him his current self is intriguing. I enjoyed following the various constants through-out his life like friends or tastes. Most of his memories revolve around his relationship with the love of his life, who happens to be a non-neurotypical woman. This is an interesting and generally underrepresented theme. I found most of their interactions to be endearing. Very rarely the game might also timidly explore almost philosophical questions (who gets to decide the value of one's own life, everyone wishes they were brought up differently, etc.), although these aspects aren't really spelled out in the dialogue (which is not a bad thing either).
These rare highlights are unfortunately eclipsed by the much more frequent [u]bad writing[/u]: The player characters (scientists) are very inconsistent and seem to freely swap traits. There are very frequent boundary transgressions. The game does a poor job of separating the memory world from the in-game "real" world and quite often even shatters the fouth wall to the actual real world in painful ways. The pop-culture references are cringy and strangely out-of-place (the game often alludes to the plot taking place decades in the future). Frequent attempts at humour rarely fit and even interfere with sombre or romantic moments. Nonsensical events take place, just for the sake of blatantly lampshading later parts of the game. The plot is mostly advanced through contrivances and deus ex machina interventions. Even so almost all the twists are predicable. Except for the ending, where the game goes over-the-top and pulls the rug out from everything that has happened previously by introducing severe mental illenesses to characters who previously seemed quite healthy. The resolution then comes through a completely artificial conflict between the two scientists. For me it felt like the last 45min just absolutely went off the rail. The writers even managed to retroactively break the quite well-rounded character of the wife ([spoiler]Why would she fold hundreds of origami rabbits instead of simply confronting him about his faulty memory? She's not the type to drop subtle hints and hope for him to miraculously improve after he stood with her through her diagnosis. She should be used to having better memory and a more rational appraoch than him and not fall into a deep crisis over it.[/spoiler])
The game even mentions that an in-universe film called "To the Moon" might be considered pretentious - but how about fixing your plot instead of lampshading its flaws? There are several inaccuracies and insanities, which can be explained by much of the game taking place within (faulty) memories. But that honestly gave me the impression of lazy writing more than I found it a compelling and well thought-out explanation. This also highlights how nothing we see can be taken for granted, as it is only based on the subjective view of one character. I found several other characters more interesting than the main patient, but we are stuck to his memories. The premise, some themes and characters were quite interesting, the over-all writing was just a bit too aimless and not well-rounded enough. I think the last twist was honestly too much and I could have done without it.

In [b][u]conclusion[/u][/b] the game's music is really good, the visuals are decent and the writing is compelling, smart or cute at times. On the other hand the gameplay is severely lacking, the technical implementation is terrible and the writing is often contrived and painfully tone-deaf. I can see lots of good seeds, but the over-all result far too often made me groan in frustration to be able to recommend it. The full price seems ridiculously expensive to me, but with various sale and bundle discounts I think it comes down to a very reasonable level if you still want to check out what all the fuzz is about.

No. Just no.

I wanted SO MUCH to like this game. But the hamfisted plot and the shallow characters that try to pass themselves off as "deep" get in the way of any sort of emotion the game tries to muster up. A lot of the plot feels like its been cheaply designed in order to wring tears out of everybody - and as a result, the game NEVER turly earns its tears, only being able to cheaply grab them through false emotions and false characters.
 
And what false charactes they are. For example, there is a character that is defined almost exclusively by her mental affliction. (I am trying to avoid spoilers here for the people who haven't played the game yet, but I will have a section on spoilers at the very bottom of this review for people who have beaten it already.) Anyway, there is pretty much nothing to that character - her personality and actions merely come off as side effects of her affliction. Where's her feelings? Where's her personality? They're not there. 

And on top of that we have the grossly manipulative plot - look, here's a song you can cry to that has  two notes!!! Aren't you so endeared because it's two notes?!?!? And, Hey, we have this actress character who won't stop being pretentious and preachy about what she has to say!!!!! Isn't she DEEP?!?!?!?!? And hey, here's this character with a sad fate that we bring up with no foreshadowing whatsoever AT THE VERY END OF THE GAME!!!! Doesn't that make you SAD?!? Point is, the game is trying so hard to show itself off as having a "DEEP STORY" that it, ironically, reveals its own shallowness and the flaws of its own plot.

All the annoying rage aside, the shame of To the Moon is that it could very well have been a good game. The setup itself is very well-done, and could have very well been a breeding ground for all sorts of truly emotional stories. There are a couple of admittedly charming moments (a talk on Doctor Who, in particular, actually did make me smile inside). And the game has very well done 16-bit-esque graphics. However, all of these little 'good' things about the game do barely anything to get away with the bad taste of the story and the game as a whole.

Some people might complain that the gameplay, which pretty much consists of collecting hidden objects to get to the next memory and then solve an fairly easy tile puzzle, is barely even there, and that is also true. I am not opposed to a near-complete lack of gameplay if the game's story is well-done.........but, as I have of course mentioned before, the story feels manipulative and its emotions feel unearned. 

In the end, I would say that if you really want to play To the Moon - go right ahead and see for yourself what you think of it. To the Moon is, at the very least, a mildly intriguing experiement on how to tell a story within a game, and it must be experienced for oneself before one can really, truly judge it. And who knows what you'll think? You might even outright love the game. But - try to consider, if you can or if you want to, how desperately the game tries to wring tears out of the player, and don't be entirely shocked if you have a disappointed reaction like I did.

As I mentioned vaugely in the review, I was extremely annoyed by [spoiler]how River was portrayed as being defined almost entirely by her autism.[/spoiler] As someone who has [spoiler]a few, diagnosed pinches of Asperger's Syndrome,[/spoiler] it annoys me how [spoiler]River[/spoiler] felt less like an actual, real person and more like a checklist that ticks off all the [spoiler]symptoms of autism[/spoiler] one by one. The character of [spoiler]Isabelle[/spoiler] also felt like an extremely manipulative way to force the player to relate with somebody [spoiler]with autism,[/spoiler] especially when she did nothing but preach and preach about [spoiler]autism[/spoiler] in general.

On top of that, some of the game's philosophies on [spoiler]autism[/spoiler] felt like a huge slap in the face to me. Am I "concealing" myself in any way if [spoiler]I don't show myself as autistic, especially if people will judge me as soon as they know that I am?[/spoiler] Am I so detached as to [spoiler]think of a lighthouse as more of a person than actual people?[/spoiler] Do I [spoiler]keep completely silent about childhood memories for no reason at all?[/spoiler] These sorts of things in the game's story are not how I behave at all in real life, and not how any kid I've seen [spoiler]with autism[/spoiler] has behaved either. (There is a "devil's advocate" argument there in that [spoiler]every child with autism of any sort is affected by it in different ways,[/spoiler] but I have a very hard time believing that any of them would be [spoiler]as detached as River is in the game[/spoiler] without some sort of extreme personal tragedy.)

I do realize that in the main review, I do kind of come off as a bit of a heartless a-hole. But this comes from anger at how - there's no other word for it - unrealistic the game's [spoiler]portrayal of autism[/spoiler] is. I do appreciate that [spoiler]some of the money that the game has received is going toward charities for autism[/spoiler] - but the fact is, this game is the same type of BS that I've been getting for years in [spoiler]dumb social thinking classes for autistic kids (I finally got out of these classes a while back, but I had to deal with them until I was a junior in highschool, and even then pretty much all of the autistic friends who are In high school with me are still dealing with them).[/spoiler] I honestly don't think that we, as a society, can truly deal [spoiler]with autism[/spoiler] until we all realize that the people who are [spoiler]affected by it are, actually, generally normal people, not creepy and detached freaks[/spoiler] - and I think that this game is a huge step backwards, in that the people who play this will have some skewed understanding of what [spoiler]autism[/spoiler] is, instead of seeing [spoiler]how normal the people who are affected by it actually are.[/spoiler]

(Also, [spoiler]sliping in an inexplicable identical twin at the very end[/spoiler] is TERRIBLE storytelling form. In ANY sort of story.)

[b][u] In-depth Review [/u][/b]
[b]Gameplay:[/b]
There really is not much gameplay. Besides clicking your way through episodes and then solving the same type of puzzle in between said episodes, there are only a handful of cheap, cheesy game like moments tacked on. While that is frustrating enough in itself, the lack of gameplay is worsened by the terrible interface, the whole game is pretty clunky, I can't believe how off the mouse detection seemed at times. 

[b]Story:[/b]
The story is the only saving grace for this game, and even it has some really weak areas. The serious story elements are actually quite good and can make one stop and think. However, those moments are almost always ruined by the asinine dialogue of the main protagonists. Supposedly you are controlling two doctors, but they sound much more like middle school children. I don't mind having some comedic relief especially in such a somber story, but the balance is off and it usually feels way out of place. Additionally the last half of the story felt quite predictable, it starts of pretty decently, but as you delve further in it becomes fairly easy to see what's going to happen next. It's possible I was just making lucky guesses, but I think more likely it was some cliché elements and excessive foreshadowing. 

[b]Presentation:[/b]
As for the artistic aspects of the game, I'd say sub-par at best. The old-school graphics are fine for the purpose of the game, but a lot of it is very ugly and plain looking, sepia tone is definitely overused. There are a few cut-scenes with a different art style and there is just no redeeming quality to them either, no unique artistic style, nor charm, nothing. There's also a sequence with a “closeup” of one of the doctors and rather than create a new sprite for the closeup it appears they used the same little sprite and just magnified it, causing the whole sequence to look really terrible. I don't understand how the music receives so much praise, while it's not terrible and fits well with the game it's repetitive

The story echoes "Eternal sunshine of the Spotless mind" a bit, with a similar memory based plot.Basically, you play as two characters who are going through a terminally ill man's memories to give him his dying wish. 

The story drags on at times to the point where I wanted to quit, with some really preachy themes, even touching on the tumblr-esque "neurotypical privilege" to a point. Unfortunately, too, this story's very much about the destination, not the journey. You'll trudge though some really boring scenes for the third act, when the payoff finally arrives. 

The gameplay's pretty non-existant, too. Which, really shouldn't be a complaint in this genre of game, but some of the mini-games such as a part where you play whac-a-mole control poorly and you really just want to get back to the main story. 

I also really hope you like the OST, because it'll be repeating itself. Alot. I think I heard the track " For River" every other scene or so. It didn't really bother me, but it's very noticable, and I can see people getting a bit annoyed by it.

The memespouting male doctor as comedic relief also completely ruins any tension or drama aside from a specific scene involving him. 

tl:dr  - It's not bad, per se, but you're investing around two and half hours of your time for around a fifteen minute "pay-off". The story's slow at times, and has conflicting themes. The OST is fantastic, but repetitive. Gameplay works as point and click, but some of the "Action" scenes with the keyboard control terribly.

Overall, I'd give this game like 6/10
