So To the Moon is one of those games that seemed to have a pretty unanimously positive customer perspective.  The reviews of this game cumulate at a very high rating, noting that it's "simple...full of heart", "absolutely beautiful", and as put by Eurogamer: "How do I explain why it's brilliant without spoiling what makes it so?"  The conclusion that can be drawn from these reviews is that To the Moon is a touching story game with little actual gameplay (since the actual gameplay isn't mentioned anywhere).  OH BOY.  Regardless, I had played some games like that before and I had actually enjoyed them, so I grabbed this at a low price and decided to complete it.  My conclusion after beating it:

To the Moon is an absolutely awful game that I believe would have been much more interesting had it been made in to a graphic novel or animated film.  The few game elements that exist are very poorly executed.  Movement itself can be frustrating and glitchy when using a mouse (I frequently found my character not responding as I expected when clicking where I wanted him to go, and at one point I had managed to walk in to the clouds and I could not get down), the search quests are horrid, and all of the other 'minigames' are trivial and completely out of place.  So, if the bare-bones gameplay elements are minimal and poorly-executed, why bother making this a game at all?  You spend most of your time clicking through conversations anyway; does that make things any more interesting?  I don't think it does at all, and by the end of the 4th hour I was completely overwhelmed at how tiring To the Moon was.  I can't believe that a GAME reviewed by GAME CRITICS recieved such high ratings for nothing other than its PLOT when the GAMEPLAY was this horrid.

Now I don't think anyone beat To the Moon and said to his or herself: "To the Moon was one of the most invigorating gameplay experience of the past year" or anything close to that, so the game was made great by the story (as shown by other reviewers).  Now I must admit that through most of the game I was very touched by the events that transpired; I will reluctantly admit that I teared up at a few moments.  The journey to the end, in terms of plot, was very respectable and  despite the childish "charm" of all the characters and the "click through the words" cutscenes I managed to actually enjoy that particular element.  I would never have given the game a 10/10, but perhaps a 6/7/8.  That was until I beat the damn thing

(SPOILERS BELOW)

To the Moon's story fails in how it wraps up the tale that it tells. You essentially spend the entire game re-living various aspects of a man's life in order to determine why he wants to go to the moon, seeing all of the experiences he'd had over the years that shaped who he was, suffered through major hardships of his life only to erase those from his memory at the end of the game so you can complete your job.  I practically threw my hands up in the air in disbelief when I realized that's how the game was going to end.  The ONLY REDEEMING ASPECT that To the Moon had going for it was smuthered out in the last minutes of this awful title and I would not recommend it to you unless you are the kind of person that likes to marvel at laughably bad titles.

Freebird Games put a lot of care into this game's aesthetics, with a careful choice of visual assets and music that successfully evokes melancholy, nostalgia, and the love and heartbreak of a lifelong relationship. I wish the studio had been more confident in this approach, because it then undermines this with a constant dialogue of ironic commentary and insults, as well as the regular insertion of ultra-simple puzzles that do nothing to complement the story. This even manifests as a genre clash: the human-focused realism of the main plot, and the science fiction trappings of the two corporate memory-hackers that you play as, adding technobabble and loading screens of fake code and game mechanics that do nothing to complement the main plot.

This clash of genre comes to a head in the conclusion, where the scientists stop just observing the man's lifetime of memory and start to alter it. But the game hadn't really convinced me that this virtual space is meaningfully "real" — you aren't changing reality, only what he remembers in his final moments. Does this matter? Is this ethical, even with his permission? What about the people who are no longer accurately remembered in his memories — should they get a say? The game shirks these questions and make the stakes about the man's true desires versus the corporate obligation to fulfilly a contract. This isn't the most thrilling conflict, and in the end the game has its cake and eats it too anyway.

Despite its flaws, the game's narrative is pretty polished and manages to portray a romantic relationship as both life-defining in a probably-positive way, but entangled in decades of trauma and fundamental disagreement. That's a pretty uncommon topic for a video game to cover, and I'm curious what the game would have been like as a "walking simulator" through this man's life, without any trappings of memory-altering machines and snarky scientists. Hopefully the creators learned in later games to play to their strengths (evocative atmosphere and linear narrative), and not to add an overabundance of punchlines and some skeletal game mechanics just to fit existing molds.

I have seen many people recomend this game due to its emotional story, it is sort of sad sure but man it is not a good game in any way. I ran into 2 gamebreaking bugs along the way that prevented me from continuing, being fixed by a restart which lost some progress. The game also trys to pad itself to make it seem longer than a short 3act, 3 hour story.

[h1]Art[/h1]
The game has very sub indie pixel art. And a handful of digitially painted seens which looked rushed and pulled me out of the game world when they did appear. It seems that pixel artists just added a noise filter to everthing they could. It almost hurts to look at some objects. There are also several charecters in the game where they seemed to have applied a noise filter and not toned down the saturation of the noise, resulting in a few charecters being covered in rainbow speckles.
========================
The one redeeming aspect of the games art is the soundtrack which was one of the only things keeping me playing. It is the only thing that pulled emotion out of the dialog, which is very bad as well. But this was ruined several times by having a very hard transition to a different track often for the sake of comedic releif.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
It is a game so how does it play? Very poorly. For an rpgmaker game the keyboard controls feel slugish and the mouse controls are infuriating. For the amount of needless walking around the game makes you do the mouse controls feel like they are working against you. You left click to walk, very simple how could it be bad. When walking long distanced you need to click on an icon that takes you to a different scene. The problem lies with the screen always moving the camera is locked to the grid that the charecters walk making the camera jerk as the charecters change direction. There is no smoothness to it making it difficult to click on things while moving. This tied with the charecters slow walking speed and long padded distances makes it feel like you are just waiting and waiting to just get on with the task at hand. The keyboard controls for walking don't feel as bad but the distanced are so long and the speed so slow it is just easier to wait on the mouse.
========================
The puzzles which are placed through the entirety of the first Act are the only type of "gameplay" this game has. You walk around placing the mouse on random objects that act as puzzle pieces, after you collect the necessary amounts you play a really easy puzzle which can be won by randomly clicking around ten times. You do this around twenty times. It is just a time killer a very boring one at that.
========================
Object placement in this game is horrid as well there was one instance where I though my game was soft locked, you normally click on charecters to talk to them or listen to them. This speech icon was just placed on the ground in the middle of to spaced out charecters. Several times throughout the game I had trouble finding the puzzle piece because they didn't even have an icon. The game also pads itself with really long camera pans and slow movement speed on long backtracking paths. With many reused areas that made me hate walking along them again and again. 

[h1]Story and Dialog[/h1]
The game is well know for its sad story. I did not feel a strong enough connection to the charecters throughout the short 3 hours expierence. My connection to them was just barely strong enough for me to drudge through the awful two main charecters dialog to even finish the game. The reason I feel I had no connection the the charecters is due to half the game being a very bad puzzle game. I was hoping Acts 2 and 3 would payoff for waiting through Act 1 but it did not.
========================
I'm going to talk about the dialog now and oh is it bad. Even the non cheesy "comedic" dialog feels like a middle schooler's essay for english class. It is ok but not amazing. But the dialog between the main playable charecters is awful. The game was made in 2009 and it dates itself hard. The writers seemed to have a hard on for name dropping things. They talk about Doctor Who, Animorphs, Google, and many many others. It is just awful and makes the game feel straight out of Tumblr. The game told me to just google something about the Animorphs books after I answered incorrectly. It is so hard to take the sad story seriously when they through garbage references at you.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
The games cult-like following does not hold up, even when overlooking the dated nature of the game. It is not fun and its story simply is not good enough to make up for how awful it is to play. Its so short and filled with padding with its story loosley tossed throughout at 2009 meme and joke ridden trainwreck. This game is not fun, and its story not very good. It wanted to be sad but the only things I was sad about was wasting a few dollars on this. If you do want to expierence its still after reading this whole review just watch a long play on youtube, it wasn't worth my time.

[h1]Final Score:[/h1]
[h1]5/10 Didn't even make me cry[/h1]

It's hard to like someone who insults Rosalene for being a woman while making pop culture references such as Doctor Who.
Rosalene isn't spared either. Throughout the story, she is consistent enough to be likable until a certain point later in the story. I will spare the spoilers to a later part of this review, but the decisions she made in the later chapter felt out of character and illogical to what has happened in the story. 

After this point, I will be spoiling parts of the story, so if you are interested of playing the story I wouldn't recommend reading any further.

Throughout the story, we experienced John Wyles's memories that focuses on his relationship with River Wyles, his wife, so that Watts and Rosalene can find the answer to the mystery of why John Wyles wants to go to the moon and as well as linking memories together for easier manipulation. You later find out that the reason why is because if John & River Wyles ever get separated, they would head to the moon to meet up and get back together. But due to some memory blocking drugs to prevent John from remembering his brother, Joey, dying, he forgot his promise to River to meet up at the moon.

After that point, the story made sense. The objective felt clear, remind John in a later memory so that it might cause him to remember his promise to River to maybe prevent his wife from constantly making paper rabbits over the years. And maybe some form of clarity and happiness from knowing that piece of information. But instead, Rosalene made the conscious decision to delete/move River away from John's early memories so that John and River don't meet. Which for some reason prevented Joey from being ran over, despite River having no influence of the event. And which caused John to pursue his dreams into going to NASA, to go to the moon. And coincidentally enough, River joined NASA at the same time so they were able to go to the moon together despite not seeing each other for a decade or two.

It felt like the writer(s) of this story got lazy in the end and decided to slap a "somehow it works" sticker at the end. The ending of the game felt undeserved.

You play as a pair of scientists that will be exploring a man's life. Going back through it at the key moments that lead to explain why he wanted to go "To the Moon." It seems to be a common theme in reviews to this game that it might move the player to tears.  I didn't find that to be the case, but I might believe that it would bore the player to tears.  I think this might be better rehashed as a simple walk-through interactive story kind of game, because the "game" components are severely lacking.  The basic notion is that you play as one of a pair of scientists brought to a dying man's bedside to install in his mind the memories of having gone to the moon.  It is an interesting premise and in a different medium, I would likely have enjoyed it.  

The way the game unfolds is that you watch a cut-scene providing a bit of story then are left wandering around to find memory-triggering objects.  When you've collected the objects, you bring them to a portal and solve a simple puzzle involving toggling rows and/or columns of an image until the whole image lines up properly.  There is no conflict for the player to resolve, nor is there much interplay between the game elements and the puzzle elements (to be clear, the objects collected and images revealed are often references to parts of the story, but the player's presence is one merely of observation rather than interaction).  

The graphics are very good, however, in a style similar to and quality comparable to some of the best rpg's and overhead hack'n'slash adventures of the 16 bit era.  Dialog is similarly on par with games of that era.  I found it generally too corny but it was definitely true-to-style of 16 bit JRPG translations (I find those generally too corny, as well).  The music is well-done but overdone.  There is solemn piano piece that, while pleasant to listen to a few times, starts to really grate in a depressing way in extended sessions.  

Bottom line:  There's no game to the game.  I appreciate the dev's willingness to take a leap on an experimental concept but it ultimately fell flat for me.  I think perhaps the concept would be more suitaed to a passive medium like film or prose, or that the idea should have been worked to incorporate the player into the story in a way that make's the player's role more integral.  I got about a third the way through the game and never really felt any connection to the story unfolding or to the characters shown.  As a result, I just wasn't enjoying the time I spent playing To the Moon (it felt at least twice as long as the > 2 hours steam reports I played) and as a result, I gave up on it.

To the Moon is a game about two scientists who can create false memories, and use this to fulfil the dying wish of those on their deathbeds. In order to understand why their client, John, wishes to go to the moon, they must work backwards from his memories, which leads to the story unfolding as they delve deeper into his past. This is certainly an interesting premise, and a unique way of telling a story about the regrets one might have at the end of their life. 

The actual gameplay part of this game is extremely minimal, with the majority being pointing and clicking or solving simple puzzles. 
The rudimentary tile flipping puzzles needed for each memento was particularly egregious, as they felt extremely out of place with the story and seemed to only serve to waste time. In fact I grew to dread the repetitive nature of collecting 5 memory orbs and solving the tiles as I knew it was coming. My least favourite part about this game ended up being the gameplay, which is disappointing to say the least. 

The artwork is good, with detailed sprites that effectively convey the complex emotions the game seeks to display, but the rudimentary tools used to create the game unfortunately make it feel dated, such as in the control scheme, which is clunky to say the least. There is also no option to change settings such as controls or resolution. While I understand that these constraints are the result of the game engine, they must nevertheless be pointed out. 

The ultimate question though is: why was this story told through the medium of video games? What choices do the player ultimately have? What separates one player’s experience from another’s? I could have watched a playthrough of this game instead of playing it myself and got the exact same experience. 

While I acknowledge and appreciate the game’s ambition, it's frustrating seeing it fall short of excellence in just about every category. While the story is good, it is not good enough to justify suffering through it’s lackluster gameplay, and for that reason I have chosen not to recommend this game.

TTM is not a game, per se, but more of a collection of cutscenes. This is fine, because it is heavily story driven.

Story - 5/10

The dialogue is boring at best and the majority of time incredibly cringey. References to Animorphs feel out of place. The dialogue is full of colloquialisms and phonetic spellings which are awful.

Sound - 10/10
The soundtrack for this game is amazing and it's only saving grace. Mostly piano based, which works nicely with the dialogue and triggers an emotional connection. Unfortunately for TTM, that's the only good part of the game.

I paid 1.99 for TTM and finished it in two sittings in about 3 hours. I feel like that's a fair value for what I paid, but I wouldn't pay much more. In my opinion this game is completely overrated and feels more like a high school play than a 'brilliant' game.

First lets start with the surface level reasons, the stuff that hurts enjoyment but could be looked over by those who enjoy it:
Controls: The controls are just plain bad, if you use the keyboard the map is designed in a grid (as in 1 press up goes one block) however the actual design of the area does not make this clear, causing keyboard controls to feel floaty, as if when you let go of the button the character will continue moving until they reach the next grid block. The mouse controls a little better with characters auto moving to where you click, but when switching surfaces or rooms they will randomly stop despite having more to move towards; overall it just controls poorly.
Art Style: I know this one is just an opinion and I'm sure many will disagree but I just really don't like the art style; I can't really put a finger on why but it just rubs me the wrong way.

So now for the more pressing reasons why I don't like this:
Dialogue: This game isn't funny; the character's say cutesy jokes and puns so so often (especially Dr. Watts) but they just arent funny, I cringed through so much of it. Emotion: All of the big emotional moments felt pointlessly manipulative; often having important bits of information or character motivation hidden simply for a twist later.
Theme: I also disagree with the point the game tries to push about manipulating the past to be happy but I wont go into detail because spoilers.

Overall I really disliked this game, I really wanted to like it, and I have heard nothing but positive regard from others but I just cannot see why. [b]To the Moon[/b] is a single player adventure story game in the style of old spirited JRPGs.  You play as two scientists whose job is to implant memories to a dying man, fulfilling his last wish to have gone to the moon.  

The gameplay in To the Moon is virtually non-existent; while you do control the characters’ movements, the game is, essentially, on rails, sans occasional simple puzzles.  The graphics are sprite-based pixel graphics very familiar to gamers of the 90’s.  They are conventional and utilitarian, but not stylized or impactful.

So, the gameplay and visual elements aren’t fantastic, but what about the story?  Well, that is certainly the highlight of this game.  Without spoiling, the story is pretty interesting and effective and keeps you engaged.  There’s some good characterization and some interesting observations.  

This is a difficult game to “rate” - I’m sure that there will be people who really like this game, and I think it is to be lauded for its original story and scrappy origin of development.  Judging it for what it is - a very small indie game that takes 3.3 hours to play, it’s fine.  The biggest glaring flaw with it for me is that it just doesn’t need to be a video game.  The creator took the tools at their disposal to create a game that told their story, but really, this doesn’t need to be a video game, or gain anything from being a video game.  You could imagine the entire game played by a bot and just watching it, but in that case, it’s a mediocre movie.  Elements unique to gaming (chance, choice & agency, etc…) are just missing here, so it’s hard to feel like it is a good game to me.  But also, I mean, it’s a game that costs a dollar!  

If you’re in the mood for an interesting story and a very casual and short gaming experience, check it out!  I have not played the successors of this game, but I feel that if they incorporate more gaming elements and continue developing interesting and original ideas they could be could, and that their future is certainly worth paying attention to.

To the Moon is shockingly bad. It's far from the worst game I've ever played, but this is genuinely some of the least I've enjoyed a game in a good long while.

There are two main culprits you can point the finger at, and their names are Eva Rosalene and Neil Watts. The protagonists, especially Neil, are insufferable. Instead of coming off as the lovable bickering old colleagues they were clearly supposed to be, these two just feel downright cruel and nasty. They can't let any moment pass without a snide comment or forced, dated reference and it completely ruins any immersive moments the game might have had. Their struggles with the ethical implications of what they're doing at the end of the game don't feel believable because I genuinely do not have any reason to believe they actually care about the situation or what they're doing because they've taken nothing seriously so far. 

The story these two are so bent on ruining isn't that great either. For the first half of the game, I was genuinely invested. Johnny's portrayal as a less than perfect man who fetishized River's autism is something weird and special and other and ultimately couldn't understand her and hurt her was compelling. The depiction of their relationship made my skin crawl, which I assumed is how I was supposed to feel. I wanted to see how the game would handle helping a man who loved someone very deeply but never really understood them for they were and his last attempt to make things right.

So when the game got to the big twist, I was bitterly disappointed. Johnny and River's relationship struggles are no longer about the two of them failing to overcome fundamental differences in how neurotypical and neurodivergent people think, River literally remembers something Johnny doesn't because he had a secret dead twin all along and took magic memory loss pills to forget his early childhood. That's boring! It absolves Johnny of responsibility for fetishizing River's otherness and not seeing her as a person! It's a stupid twist! It just left an awful sour taste in my mouth and made the happy ending feel completely unearned. It wasn't a happy ending for River, and the game never acknowledges that. 

There's a few other little things. All the supporting characters feel pointless. I would have loved to know more about Isabelle, but she's only present for a few scenes. Lily and the kids are cute, but they never really do anything. Johnny's doctor gets to join us for the big happy ending, but we never even learn their name. And I know this game got sequels so maybe it gets addressed there, but what was up with the game randomly introducing Neil's opioid addiction and not bringing it up again??

The gameplay too is really only there for the sake of it. The puzzles are fine, but didn't need to be there at all. The music is pretty good though. That and some of the first half of the game are the only things worth saving. This game squandered every interesting idea it had and was annoying and uncomfortable about it the whole way through. Even as a product of its time, I cannot bring myself to like it.

To the Moon feels like it is intended to be sentimental and touching, and evidently for some people it was. For me, though, the sentimentality felt like a strange veneer on a storyline that could more properly be considered horror or grim tragedy. That kind of incongruity made the game feel unsettling, and not in a good way - more like in a "am I crazy, or does this make no sense" kind of way. I bought this game on steam daily sale after I'd had a few drinks. Not my best purchase. I normally don't play games in this style. To The Moon is a retro, jrpg style indie game that is completely story driven, all three of which (retro, jrpg style, story driven) I usually stay away from, so I was surprised it engaged me so. Even though I couldn't put it down for the 3ish hours it takes to complete, I do feel it's extremely overrated and only ok. Here's my thoughts.

First the easy part to critique, the gameplay. The gameplay sucks. You're viewing your characters in top down jrpg style like an old final fantasy game but you move by clicking the mouse and then you have to click items but the controls are finicky. You'll be clicking an item and sometimes your guy moves there, sometimes he won't. It just doesn't work right. Then a lot of it is repetitive and cumbersome when really you just want to get through to the next part of the story. The gameplay is a hindrance in most cases. Also it's not consistent at all. Some chapters you do a lot of clicking and searching then other ones are full out cutscenes with zero gameplay. I don't understand it.

Second the presentation. The graphics are fine for what it's supposed to be, though I don't get all nostalgic for old school 16 bit graphics. I think this game could've be way better with something new and fresh like hand drawn flash animation or cartoon stylized. But the devs made their choice and it's good within its limits. But my issues with the presentation are this story makes so much more sense as a book or a movie. The story tries to get emotional and make you feel empathy and invested in characters but being a video game it just can't develop. I really appreciate developers trying to push boundaries of gaming and I'm fascinated by the philosophical discussion of narratives and art form in video games, and this one tries very heroically but ultimately fails for me. If it was a book that had more time to flesh out relationships and personalities or a movie that had actors to impress those upon the viewer I think it would work. Reading 16 bit dialogue though leaves something lacking for me.

That's why I don't understand the reviews that say this game is a masterpiece, it's so evocative, it made me cry. I'm like really? So a couple 16 bit characters sharing 30 lines of typed dialogue is enough to establish an emotional connection for you? I think you need to get out into the real world more. The story is kind of like the movie inception where this company can change your memories the moment before you die so you can have the life you've always wanted in your mind and die happy. It follows these two scientist employees who are trying to help this old guy rewrite his memories to go to the moon, his dying wish.

I also had serious issues with the story once I thought about it in depth a bit. The whole point was that his bonds with River were so strong that she remained in his mind even when removed, that he would do anything to be with her. Just like how he wanted to go to the moon in the first place even though he couldn't remember exactly why. And in the end they hold hands as they reach the moon and he dies. Ok, fine, so he loved her a lot and his love conquered all except it really didn't because the whole freakin thing was IN HIS HEAD. River is still dead, she still chose building the house over the treatment and left him. He still had a ton of pain in his life, but it's supposed to be all ok because he doesn't remember it? That's what I don't like at all, how our imposed virtual reality now trumps what actually happened. Although I guess maybe the devs were doing this on purpose to push the question of what is reality and is it only in the mind and memories? I appreciate the question but the story felt more like the point was , aww look how much he loved her and now everything's alright, and I just didn't feel that way. She still chose to build the house and die. They never actually met on the moon.

The music I also had issues with. Not because it's bad, cus it's not, it's quite good. It's beautifully simplistic and I enjoyed it as background video game music. It fits the story and mood well. But reviews rave about it like it's a Beethoven symphony. It's not that great or talented, and the one with lyrics was borderline emo rocker ballad. I feel like this generation doesn't know what great music is anymore. The music fits the game well and is good, but it's still extremely overrated.

Overall overrated game experience. If the game moves you to tears I feel like you should have a serious discussion with yourself over why. Did you relate to a specific part of the game? Did some of what's in it happen to you in real life? Because that I can understand but otherwise I think those with that kind of response are overreaching because the want to feel a connection to something. There's far better, deeper game stories out there with better characters to feel connection to than these.

The story was interesting, but predictable. The characters were interesting, but flat — and not just because they're 2D. The puzzles started out interesting, but quickly got repetitive. By the third act, I was agonizing for the game to be over so I could make dinner. 

My best friend and younger sister recommended this game to me. They adore this game. How am I supposed to tell them I don't?

I remember my sister mentioned that she thought I'd appreciate the game because I'm a writer. 

Well, it's actually only made it easier to pick out the reasons I don't. After some deliberation, I think the reason I and many others weren't able to connect to the characters can be confined to a list of pretty simple issues:

[b]First:[/b] the controls are janky as hell. If you can get past the awful moving controls and figure out the weird right/left clicking mechanics, then you're a champ. I immediately noticed, however, that this game had no options menu. There was no way to make the game windowed, no way to switch the arrow keys over to WASD, and no way to in-game adjust volumes. It wasn't exactly a great first impression. 

Further, the actual "game play" (if you can even call it that) is somehow both threadbare and confusing. You get used to what you're supposed to do pretty quickly, which would be fine if it weren't that what you're supposed to do gets pretty dull just as fast. Clicking on objects that slightly stand out and fixing puzzles in a few more clicks isn't exactly engaging game play, which only hurts a gamer's immersion. 

And then there are times when you get stuck and just start clicking on [i]everything...[/i] 

The game previews itself to the gamer as an interactive, story-driven novel. But it's not. It's a movie occasionally interrupted with bad movement controls and very strange scene set up that mark flowers as impassable terrain. 

This is all more or less easy to look over. However...

[b]Second:[/b] The doctors. I've seen a few reviews saying their humor feels forced and distracts too much from the story. Myself, though, I actually enjoyed their commentary. They often voiced what I was thinking, and their dialogue was used at times to foreshadow large character beats in the story. However, by the third act when Eva went off the rails, I realized why I was having trouble connecting with them: they had no personal goals.

The doctors immediately introduce themselves as the comedic levity in this heart-warming tearjerker. That works well and good, but even Guy from [i]Galaxy Quest[/i] has a character arc and fulfills his own thematic hero's journey. The doctors are completely without.

Get the job done and over with. Grab a cup of coffee and move on to the next patient. They say this in so many words multiple times between the beginning of the game and the end. 

It leaves very little room for me to root for them or, by extension, for Johnny's dream. There's no interconnection, nothing to tie these characters together, so the journey feels like "just another job" but with a few mildly-interesting hiccups.

This leads me to...

[b]Third:[/b] The character resolutions are poor and hollow, and some are completely nonexistent. 

Eva is mentioned to have a moment-to-moment life motto to get her through her job. I was hoping that seed would be watered enough to grow into an arc. However, it's never expounded, challenged, or resolved. Neil is mentioned to be cold and calloused toward his patients. That's not explored, challenged, or resolved either (though he came closer than Eva when he challenged her over the contract they had to fulfill; however, she took control of the situation, stealing that character moment from Neil and replacing it with literal zombies). 

Honestly, their personalities are simply flat; just as 2-dimensional as the stylized world. And no matter how cute or comedic a scene might be, I was unable to stand behind them and root for their stories because they didn't have one. 

Moving on, John and River. 

River's story had the most nuance; though, that's not saying much. By the end of the game, I had an idea of what had happened to her, and I feel like I understand what I'm supposed to understand about her, but it's only superficially explored and certainly not resolved. In fact, the ending felt anti-climatic to me, because John certainly never had the moment of realization concerning River that the game worked so hard for the gamer to achieve. 

And John: his story is complicatedly wonky. His dream of being an astronaut, as I mentioned, right from the start feels empty and silly. The characters even say as much. By the time we find out what it stems from, there's so much baggage unpacked that his dream of going to the moon feels like a red herring from the real resolution we could be searching for. Neil even has dialogue talking about this, so I know the writers behind the game were aware of the issues unpacking so many metaphorical bags posed. The end of the game had one bow, but hundreds of ribbons. One origami rabbit, and [i]boxes[/i] of unfulfilled paper.

I won't get into details for the sake of spoiling the story for others (because the game is cute despite its flaws, and you could at least watch a Let's Play if you want to enjoy the positive aspects of the story and game); overall: John and River's arc isn't finished by the end of the game, but glossed over and slapped with a big ol' NASA sticker. It's unsatisfying.

Lastly: The third act is just a movie. You can't pause, save, or escape, either. So have water and snacks close at hand. And when you see the third act text pop up, take a bathroom break. It's like half an hour. 

[b]That being said:[/b]

[h2]SUMMARY[/h2]

Think Inception but with less gunfights and more melodrama.

Although To the Moon is laudable for its high concept and its willingness to explore themes of living with autism, its execution is weak due to general issues with storytelling pacing, writing, and gameplay.

[h2]STORYTELLING[/h2] 

The most glaring issue with the storytelling is the entire first act, which centers around the two point of view doctor characters stepping backwards through the memories of their patient. Unfortunately, during this portion of the game the doctors have very little active agency beyond serving as veritable exposition sponges. And at two hours (out of a total game runtime of three to four) the first act and its incremental episodes start to feel interminable. While some interesting ideas are explored during this portion (how to cope with an autistic partner), it is boring, and there is not sufficient payoff for everything introduced here.

That does not even touch upon the gameplay, which feels like barely justified busywork and makes the early pacing issues even worse.

The second and third acts work better as they are shorter and give the two player characters more to do in the story.

[h2]WRITING[/h2]

Dialog and writing are stilted and weak, and characters either are extremely bland or unbearably obnoxious. For instance, Kan Gao attempts to characterize female doctor as an acerbic hard-ass to contrast to male doctor's loveable goofball. The goal was clearly for the two doctors to have a buddy cop dynamic - catty but familiar. However, because neither female doctor or male doctor have any charisma, this falls flat, and both characters just read as insufferably lame.

[h2]TECHNICAL[/h2]

The use of the RPG Maker as a game engine does To the Moon no favors. The grid based movement is slow and stilted and results in some very odd collision detection with random scenery. Although graphically To the Moon is a very handsome game by RPG Maker standards, indie gaming culture has changed so much in the past decade that To the Moon's visual stylings feel quaint at best.

On the upside, music is pleasant and effectively used in game.

[h2]CONCLUSION[/h2]

To the Moon was widely decorated in its original release, but all of the problems the game has with story, writing, and gameplay suggest that it is a product of its time: fast forward almost a decade, and games that focus exclusively on story are no longer novel.

"A DEEP, EMOTIONAL, WELL-WRITTEN STORY."

"IT MADE ME CRY."

"ONE OF THE GREATEST INDIE GAMES EVER MADE."

"A MASTERPIECE."


...And it was with words like these that I dove into 'To The Moon' with very high expectations. I prepared myself for a mind-blowing experience...with all the overwhelming positive reviews, how could it not be? This game was going to OWN, I was convinced. So when I saw this in an attractively priced bundle, I didn't hesitate to snap it up. Unfortunately, the actual game didn't live up to the hype.

GOOD 
+ Graphics are decent for this style of game
+ Music is good, though repetitive
+ Interesting concept for the storyline (scientists going back into a dying patient's memories and recreating them to match the patient's one true desire, like granting a wish)


BAD
- Clunky controls. Imagine playing an old school SNES JRPG with a mouse. 
- Lack of ENGAGING gameplay. Finding the 'mementos' and completing the ensuing simple flip puzzle got tiresome fast, and having to complete a bunch of them to advance the storyline made me feel like I was slogging through the game after a while. This is pretty much all there is as far as gameplay, other than moving your character around and clicking through dialogue boxes. 
- Slow performance. This game wasn't optimized for modern machines. But that's due mostly to the engine it was built on, from what I've read.
- Overrated story. It had its moments, but too much cheese and seemed forced. Characters weren't fleshed out enough. Ending...was typical. And predictable.
- Not enough feels. At least for me. I was really hoping the story and characters were gonna grip me and make me bawl my eyes out, like all the reviews said. My eyes remained dry throughout.
- Zero replay value. No alternate endings. No secrets to find. No extra or hidden characters. No bonuses. You get NOTHING.

Overall...."meh". I finished the game, but it felt like a chore most of the time. With an engaging storyline, which is this game's main selling point, it would have been different. I bought this game in a bundle, and dividing the cost of the bundle with the number of games in it, 'To The Moon' came to about .60 cents; a good deal any way you slice it. Full price = hell no. At $1.99 or less = worth a shot. Still, despite all its positively glowing reviews, I can't give this my full recommendation.

[h1] Gameplay: 4/10 [/h1]
It's pretty repetitive: find all the things in the level, go to new level, rinse, repeat. That's not really too much of an issue here. This game is more story than game (an interactive movie if you will), where player interaction exists mainly to increase immersion and aid the storytelling.

[h1] Graphics: 7/10 [/h1]
It's pretty, in a 16-bit sort of way. The only problem is the icky 4:3 resolution that freaks most PC displays out and refuses to upscale reasonably. That doesn't detract too much from this game, but it sure is annoying.

[h1] Plot: 10/10 [/h1]
This game [i] is [/i] story-driven. The plot is very novel and touching. It's a real tear-jerker, but this is not $5 tearjob you get behind a Sunoco station in downtown Detroit. This game costs $10, comes to your house, wears some nice lingerie, and jerks your tears real sweet-like. A really well-crafted plot with great character development and structure.

[h1] Soundtrack: 9/10 [/h1]
The soundtrack complements the game well, and is very good in general. If you get this game, it's probably worth getting the soundtrack bundle for what little extra it costs.

[h1] Replay Value: 0/10 [/h1]
Sadly, after four hours, your $10 in-home tearjerk is over. That's it. Nothing more. No collectibles, no real achievements. You're done.

[h1] Overall: 60/100 [/h1]
As much as this game is great, it isn't really worth ten dollars for an hour-and-a-half-long visual novel that lasts four hours because it's padded for time with a "game", whatever a "game" is. Truly, it's a wonderful story, but if this story alone is worth ten dollars, then Donnie Darko should be on display in the Louvre. So, if this is on sale, go for it. Otherwise, I can't recommend it.

[b]Edit 7/2/2017:[/b] While I can't recommend this game at full price, I would highly recommend it on sale for any price below $5 or $6. It would be well worth it for the story.

The game itself looks smudged, sometimes misses screen elements, has mechanics that are introduced early on but never become relevant, and I'm almost certain some of the sounds were recycled from older games. The story is the selling point, but it can be difficult to follow (and seems to contradict itself), while the humour (which would be essential because the story hits like sledgehammer) is crude and clashes with the serious tone of the subject.

The music is good, although it's a bit short/repetitive. I'm sure there's a welcoming space in gaming for emotional stories, but if it's done [i]as a game[/i] then the interactivity, visuals, and audio would need some level of effort. Even the story had clear space for improvement, as the dialogue felt unnatural (especially when you consider the age of some the characters), and the sci-fi elements were neglected (the Space Shuttle wasn't capable of a Moon mission).

Potentially I think there were better mediums that this story could have been developed into. A good example would be [i]The Inner Light[/i] (Star Trek: The Next Generation - S5E25). They obviously lacked the budget for that, but the high ratings for [i]To the Moon[/i] (96% positive) put my expectations way too high. I don't think it was a 'bad' game. It was okay.
However, all things considered, [b]playing through this game felt a bit too much like a chore[/b] for me to recommend it to someone else.

[h1] Graphics + Soundtrack: A[/h1]

I'll start by writing that the game is pretty to look at (as pretty as RPG Maker pixel graphics can be, anyway), and even prettier to listen to. The piano soundtrack is just beautiful.

[h1] Writing: B[/h1]

The writing is solid. It's witty, and the humor is clever. To be honest, I enjoyed the humorous parts a lot more than the emotional parts of the game, which is kind of odd for a story that focuses primarily on being emotional.

[h1] Story: C+[/h1]

And yes, the story is emotional... kind of. I appreciate the uniqueness of time travelling through memories (I'm a big fan of time travel), so that was pretty cool. But the story itself is simply not memorable. It feels like a combination of 'touching' cliches. To me, personally, it felt more cheesy and predictable than actually sad... kind of like an okay-ish Hollywood movie. Maybe it's because I've been spoiled by so many deeply awesome stories in anime or in other games, but To the Moon simply wasn't gripping.

[h1] Pacing: D- [/h1]

It is also terribly slow paced. It's a 4 hour game that felt like 10. Each scene appears like it is being drawn out to the maximum, and I found myself disconnecting from the story and telling myself "Okay, I get it, let's move on" way too many times. I believe it could have been compressed into a 2 hour game without losing its essence or message.

Oddly enough, the one part that did not feel drawn out, but instead rushed, was the saddest event of the story, which doesn't make sense, as I did not have time time to feel emotional about that particular event.

[h1] Gameplay: E [/h1]

Finally, the gameplay is dreadful. Walking around with clunky controls, doing the same thing (clicking on everything to gather memories) in every scene was not fun at all. I can appreciate walking sims when the walking part isn't so awkward, but this was really rough.

Everything simply felt glitchy, even though it wasn't a bug.

[h1]Overall: C[/h1]

In conclusion, for me, To the Moon's okay story was simply not captivating enough to make up for its incredibly unpleasant game play.

[h1]To the Moon is a short and nice story, but...[/h1]

First of all, I need to say that this game has a great and emotional story with good placed surprise elements, that is supported by a very beautiful music. You really see the effort the developers put in these elements. However, there were several things which ruined the game experience for me.

One of the main issues I have with this game is the lack of actual gameplay. I'm all for lots of text explaining the story, but it needs to be wrapped around a nice and good feeling gameplay. If it isn't, what's the point of making this experience a game? The story itself could easily be told in form of a book, a comic strip, a small movie... If you call it a game, give us something to play! 
Most of the gameplay of the game can be described very easily: You go to a memory, search for a memento link to an earlier memory, look for 5 remarkable elements in the current memory, to break the barrier of the memento (it can be a plush you'd have to interact with but often you just get 1-2 elements just by entering a room, which imo is pretty lazy), solve an easy minigame, rinse, repeat. 99% of the time you have the same two party members. The replay value is very very low and a thoughtfull walkthrough only takes about 3-4h.

Another grave problem I had with this game were the characters. Only John and Eva seemed kinda human to me, the others were very shallow and I often was annoyed by their presence. Not only does this include Neil (whose jokes were often out of line, especially if you keep in mind that he's supposed to be a professional, who is dealing with very intimate memories of dying people), but also the children (who don't deserve sweets at all) and River (even after learning about her condition, I don't find her actions to be appropriate).

Last but not least, it was strange to see so many unnecessary elements given to the player. For example, the doctor gives you a device to monitor John's condition. However, I never had a situation where this devide was needed - the pulse was stable through the game and when this finally changed you had other feedback telling you this.

All in one, I'd say this game is a great addition to a humblebundle with other games and could be considered bying for 50-70% off. However, I wouldn't reccomend buying this game for the full price.

First of all, I do want to say what I like. I liked the premise of revisiting the life story of a dying man which feed into the gameplay of looking for moments in memories and the emotional depth certain items can hold throughout a lifetime. It is a novel concept that for especially the first half I liked a lot to explore.

It’s however the way this story is being told I have a problem with.

[Spoiler] And it all has to do with the characterisation of River.

For people that don’t know, I am autistic myself and that means the vast majority of my social circle is neurodivergent. I’m incredibly familiar with what makes an autistic person tic and what they’re like.

And I barely saw any of that back in River.

In fact, it actually falls into a lot of stereotypical, Rainman-like traits that alienated me. Because let me tell you, from all the autistic people I’ve met throughout my life (which like I said are a lot), not even one closely resembled River. In fact, it makes it even worse by also portraying her as mentally unstable and almost insane which I find maddening and pulled me out of the story.

Which is a shame because this whole part of the story feels unnescary and only muddles the theme of wishing your life went different with other people who were taken away from you which is a hell of a lot more powerful message.

Combine that with writing that, although very pure in its authenticity, has a tendency to remark its own story beats as cheesy and corny [i] while still wanting us to care deeply about said payoffs, [/i] and there are story moments that just either fall flat, actively annoyed me or both. [/spoiler]

Overall, although I do think To the Moon has something going for it, the novelty of its gameplay and story however wears off to a point that halfway through I really wanted this to end, especially since Before Your Eyes tells a much more focused and impactful story in half of To the Moon’s runtime.

My honest review after having just finished "To the Moon": This is an OK story told through the wrong medium, simple as that. 
The gist of the story is, a dying man wants a final "wish" granted, which is basically a personally tailored dream he receives just before death. In this case, the man wants to go to the Moon. The dream is somehow constructed by wading through his life's memories and finding the place and time where the wish first occured. However, a problem soon becomes apparent as no one, including the dying man, really knows why he wants to go to the Moon. I won't spoil the story, only say that the man has some childhood traumas that must be "sorted". 
The story is certainly emotional, just not THAT deep in my opinion; I couldn't really connect that much to the characters involved, Especially since the 2 protagonists were incredibly childish and constantly made infantile jokes during the game, destroying any mood that could have been. 

That however, is not the problem of this game - it is the game itself. The game mechanics are completely superficial: you must hunt around the man's memories for objects of particular importance to the memories. Most of these objects are important for no rhyme and reason whatsoever: a sofa, a football, an umbrella; it can be anything. When you have them all, you must solve a flip puzzle to continue. The game hardly require any cognitive facilities on the players part. 

If the story had been told as a film, or perhaps a book, I think I could have related better to it. As it stands though, I did not find it worth my time. 

Nonetheless, there is one brilliant part about the game: The music is incredible, in particular the piano piece "For River". It is beautiful, and the composer has been so nice as to make the piano sheet available. That alone was worth the price I paid for the game.

To the Moon is a story-driven point-and-click game that's about two scientists who travel into a dying man's thoughts in order to create a new set of memories for him. It has one of the best stories I've ever encountered in gaming. The portrayal of the characters - the man, who carries a lot of regrets, his wife, who suffers from an unidentified (in-game, at least) condition, and the doctors themselves - is all spot-on and reminds me a bit of the characters in a Miyazaki movie. They're all a little flawed and clearly world-worn without being characatures. This world isn't black and white.

I can tell that the story is a very personal one for the creator, and I can strongly identify with it - I share the main character's love for Animorphs, for example. The details of the story are all very realistic and resonate with me greatly.

But the gameplay brings this way down for me. You just walk around clicking on objects and occasionally playing a flip-the-tiles game. There's no challenge or thought whatsoever and the gameplay sections are unbearably dull. The only fun moment for me was the one puzzle that actually requires a little work to solve, and ironically involves obscure Animorphs trivia, which I thought was hilarious.

The story is great, yes, but it's not a story that's suited very well to an interactive medium like gaming. This should have been a short story or a short film, not a game. Let's compare it to Brothers. Now, I know it's not very fair to compare To the Moon to one of the best games of all time, but bear with me. The story in Brothers is less interesting than the story in To the Moon, but what makes it compelling is that Brothers' story is powerful specifically because it is told through an interactive medium - a game. The game's message relies on you learning to control the characters. In To the Moon, on the other hand, the attempt to shoehorn "gamey" elements into it significantly mutes the impact of the story because it interrupts it every few minutes with annoying, fiddly searching about.

So that's why this gets a thumbs down.

I have lots of thoughts about this. When I finished playing I had to go see if my partner was awake so I could complain to them about it for like half an hour. 
First, let me say, there are lots of good things about it - the music is beautiful, the core mechanic/premise is fascinating and I would totally read a book or watch a movie exploring it, the art is great. Love the random Animorphs references.
But the plot? The characters? Hate 'em. What feels like the ultimate takeaway? Unbelievably frustrating. 
Non-spoiler - I don't think it's good or respectful autism representation, partway through it feels like the game mechanics /should/ change but they stay the same, and hand-waving does not solve major plot points. 

Heavy spoilers ahead. Seriously, I'm gonna break down the whole plot. 

The timeline runs in reverse due to how the technology at the core of the game mechanic works (which, again, pretty cool!) so I am gonna address plot points in the order we encounter them, which will feel backwards. 

So his wife, River, was autistic. He never really understood her (except when he was a tiny kid, and even then he more just was open to being playful and imaginative more than he actually /got/ her) and in adulthood he is consistently frustrated/irritable about her being "so weird". When their friend calls him neurotypical he acts like it's a slur. Anytime he is faced with her being "different" he responds negatively and just wants the conversation to end so he can go back to avoiding thinking about it. When she gets diagnosed, and they're offered a book that could be helpful, he refuses to read it. (He does accommodate her in at least one way, which is to make all the clocks in the house not tick, and that is a sweet gesture) 

She's constantly wanting something from him, and she is explicitly asking questions and expecting him to know the answers and being dismissive and frustrated and silent when he cannot produce the response she wants. This is, she wants him to describe the origami rabbits she keeps folding, and he runs out of descriptors, and she just goes back to making more, like, thousands and thousands of them. Now, this could be great representation of an autistic special interest, but she doesn't seem to really enjoy it and it feels much more like a desperate pursuit of some goal that she feels compelled to do, almost more an OCD repetitive behavior. She doesn't have lots of cool facts about rabbits, she doesn't seem happy when she's making them. 

Later she needs surgery and tons of care, presumably for some other health condition since there aren't surgeries to treat autism, but they never actually say that she got diagnosed with anything else, if you didn't know better you could easily think that all these surgeries and expensive treatments were to try to "fix" her autism)
Oh also she is obsessed with this lighthouse, which their house is next to, who she names Anya and insists that he look after her and she wants the lighthouse taken care of instead of getting her surgeries and refuses treatment so that he will stay in the house next to the lighthouse and take care of it. (We have seen that by the time we are there it has boards over the windows and is in disrepair, but full of origami rabbits)
Another thing from this era is Johnny revealing some secret from long ago, River handling it "well for the most part" and then being more detached and distant after that. 

Johnny in high school tells his best friend that he wants to date River because she is weird, and he doesn't want to be "typical", and his friend points out that dating someone just because they make you seem more interesting is kinda shitty, but whatever, go ahead and ask her out. At first I thought this was the secret he reveals to her after they're already married that pisses her off, but then we get this reveal and I wonder if it might actually be about that? It's never made clear. 

Eventually, we find out that the reason Johnny never gives River the "right" description of the origami rabbits is because he has severe memory loss because he was put on beta blockers as a kid because his twin brother died in a tragic accident. The scientists break past this memory block by making his old man body in the present smell roadkill (which could be viewed as a link to Johnny and River encountering a dead rabbit at their wedding, but we have much younger memories than that, and the memory it ends up leading to is of seeing his brother hit by a car, so like... smelling the rotting flesh of this squirrel who has been laying on the blacktop for a whole day reminds him of seeing his brother get hit by a car? I guess? Gross) 

Now, we get to see what Johnny was like before the beta blockers, and the unhealthy dynamic in his family, and the fact that he actually met River once before what we previously thought was their first memory together. (the reveal of there being a twin is actually pretty well done, too, but happens at the same time as he dies, which makes it feel really icky to me) His mom clearly prefers his brother, who we now know dies, and he later has NO MEMORY OF, to the point that at their wedding his mom calls him by his dead brother's name and he still doesn't remember the brother even then.

We see him meet River and it is pretty cute! And this one conversation, which he later forgets, is apparently the basis for the entire plot of the game, all the interactions with River when they're both older, the reason he wants to go to the moon, the rabbit symbolism, and the lighthouse. They stargaze together, and make a constellation shaped like a rabbit with the moon as the rabbit's big belly, and she describes her loneliness in a very poetic (and advanced for her age, not sure if that's supposed to be an autism thing or if it's just thoughtless writing) imagery of the stars being lighthouses that are so far apart they can only see each other's light and not actually be friends, but she wants to be friends with one someday. Johnny's mom calls to him and as he leaves they promise to meet back there, and if he gets lost "we'll meet on the moon, silly!"

So one of the scientists decides this means that in order to get him to go to the moon, they have to make sure he doesn't meet River. That way, he will want to go to the moon because that is where they said they would meet. Setting aside for the moment the absurdity of someone making their entire life/career be based on a single conversation from when they were like 5 or 6, there is no conversation about what they do to prevent the twin dying-beta blocker-memory loss situation, he just lives and is around without that ever being addressed. He becomes a successful author by writing a book openly mocking his brother's desire to be an astronaut (not sure why he loses the niceness he had as a kid) and Johnny goes to become an astronaut, where suddenly River shows up! She also decided to become an astronaut to go to the moon based on interpreting a throwaway comment from childhood as a literal travel instruction. They fly to the moon and hold hands. 

See their powerful perfect love, so romantic, so great, wow, not acknowledging how this doesn't change their totally incompatible communication and emotional expression styles, the fact that he only wanted to date her because he thought she was weird and he wanted to be interesting by proximity to a weirdo, the way that he lied to her about money when he knew if she knew the truth she wouldn't behave the way he wanted her to, on and on and on they made choices that were not healthy or appropriate, and we're supposed to just forget about that, and pretend that in this alternate timeline they would not have any of those problems? I don't buy it.

Traversing in a top down RPG style should be much more intuitive than it was here. Every time I got placed in an outdoor environment, I let out a sigh. In fact, it's games like this that have me raising a suspicious eyebrow, questioning if they deliberately added all the walking around to pad out the length of the game. It doesn't serve the experience effectively.

I'm someone that holds film to a higher regard than video games, so I have a distinctive preference between the two when it comes to certain things. For me, I need to feel my own presence in the game or have some kind of influence over the story in some shape or form, even if it's in the most minuscule way. That can be as simple as fourth wall breaks, or just some freedom to explore the environment around me. This game is aggressively linear and you have very little sway over what happens. And when the presentation is as lo-fi as this and yet requires just enough input from you to keep it moving forward, it feels like a concerted yet unnecessary effort to push the story forward and I found it hard to immerse. I didn't get the point of mashing interact on random sprites in the scene to try and unlock another memory point to progress the story. To this effect, it's very much a product of the time where Lets Plays were the preferred way to experience a game so you didn't have to do that kind of minimal interaction yourself.

Anyway, all that aside, I really did enjoy what this game tried to do. It's practically a Charlie Kaufman love letter and I dig the hell out of that. But it's bogged down by its dated engine, poor gameplay and questionable character direction. I wish I'd gotten to this one back in 2011 when it was a novelty. I know this game was one of the big champions of not only independent games as an industry, but also the whole 'Are video games an art form' debate. And while I wholeheartedly agree to that notion, this game is ironically not one I would point to for this. I would have enjoyed it more as a visual novel, a book, or even (In some alternative reality where something like this would secure a big enough budget) a movie like the ones it proudly wears on its sleeve as inspiration. But then at that point you could watch Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, or Synecdoche New York instead.

No game, upon its completion, has made me feel as disappointed and as enraged as To The Moon. What was supposed to be an emotional journey through an old man's memories to fulfill his final wish turned out to be a horribly offensive and inconsistent story that isn't subtle about its hatred. There isn't much gameplay, but I didn't mind that as the focus of the game is supposed to be on the story. The tone is all over the place. It aims to be a heartbreaking game, but the constant unfunny commentary from the two main characters (one of whom makes blatantly sexist remarks to his partner throughout the game) ruins any tension the game would otherwise build. This is one of very few games that features an autistic character (the game never directly tells you she's autistic, but it's heavily implied), but she is treated as a soulless husk whose abilities and limitations are wildly inconsistent. Every other character treats her as a problem to be solved, so it wasn't surprising to find out the developers have donated to Autism Speaks which is considered by autistic people to be a hate group. This game boasts its representation of neurodivergent minds but strips its character of her autonomy and turns her into an animal to be studied and ogled, and these are dangerous stereotypes that real autistic people already have to fight. I don't think any real autistic person was involved in the making of this game. I really wanted to like To The Moon, and the glowing recommendations and reviews I saw made me think that I would, but its disgusting sexism and autistic rep make me hate this one. I won't be recommending it to anyone, and I will be trying to remove it from my memory.

Let me say that while I don't feel as if I'd recommend this game, I'm not claiming it was a wholly unenjoyable experience. It just might not be what a lot of people are looking for, and the number of positive reviews are a bit misleading.

Positive:
-Some well-crafted storytelling, I'll admit.
-Good worldbuilding, some clever ideas.
-Positive representation of autistic characters, not a lot of misinformation that stood out to me that might have ruined that.

Negative:
-Short.
-While the story is inventive, it is also linear, and I hesitate to call To the Moon an "interactive storybook" at all, but that's the best description I can think of because it kind of falls short of being a game.
-Moving around is a chore. The characters are often slow, and you inexplicably bump into things on the map sometimes that are arbitrarily solid. (You can walk through cars, but not over flowers? Really?)
-Puzzles are simple and boring. Does not feel like much at stake. They don't really add much to the story by being there other than giving the player something active to do.
-Gameplay mostly consists of walking around and clicking things until you click on something "important." Click on enough important things and you can unlock the simple tile puzzle and move on to the next memory. There's nothing really fun about it.
-On that note it would have made sense for the game to be more passive. The components that were there seemingly just to make it "like a game" felt out of place.
-IF YOU USE THE INTENDED CONTROLS (the mouse) YOU'RE GONNA HAVE A BAD TIME. You click somewhere for the characters to go somewhere, but they often don't quite reach entirely, maybe because of an obstacle, and so it feels like the characters are never going where you want them to go. Getting to objects is exhausting. When I discovered you could use the traditional arrow keys to move and the space to interact it was a life saver.
-Too much dialogue, I hate to say. Wayyy too much bickering between the protagonists bogs down the whole game. Way too much melodramatic prosey monologuing at times, too, taking away from the impact of actually beautiful and important dialogue. Just too much. It's clumsy. You spend much of the game inundated in wooords.
-What's worse is the characterization is weak at best. Most of the characters don't have much in the way of personality, which you kind of expect from this kind of game especially if it's supposed to be carried by character interactions.
-A lot of it... was not funny. When it was trying to be funny. A lot of inward groans to be had at the unnecessary snark. (There were funny parts to be had, definitely. Most of the annoying stuff was in the dialogue between Watts and Rosalene, who as I already said, spend way too much time bickering.)
-This is a bit of a personal nitpick, but I wish, if they were going to make a game about asperger's, that they might just name it outright. I don't understand why everyone was so cagey and vague about River's "condition," it struck me as unnecessary.

Verdict: If you are going to get it, get it on sale. Then stick it out past Act 2, because that's where the story starts picking up and you don't have to put up with the puzzles and junk. Don't approach it expecting much in the way of a game, or much in the way of replay value. It's a decent story, not decent enough for me to wholly recommend the experience, but not bad enough for me to say there was nothing worthwhile about it, either.

Although this game presents itself very well and has had an overwhelmingly positive reception, I must beg to disagree. Let's start with what I liked about this game: The soundtrack. Oh my God, is it amazing! It's one of the most perfect OST-Game combinations I've ever seen! It simply ties in perfectly with the game, as if the story and the song were but one thing. Also, the story up until Act 2 is simply superb. I honestly had myself close to crying more than a few times and it deeply touched me multiple times.

But, that, as they say, is that. Nothing else good, to be honest. The graphical design is neither good nor bad, it's simply a matter of personal choice (one with which I agree). The controls/interactivity is, simply put, godawful. You get stuck on random parts of the scenery ALL THE GODDAMN TIME and the mouse control simply doesn't work for movement. The gameplay is awfully repetitive and gets annoying quite quickly and even though some might argue that 'gameplay isn't the point of this game, story is!' that isn't an excuse for a lack of interesting gameplay. The lack of multiple endings and the puzzle solving of interacting with the mementos is, in all seriousness, a letdown.

And finally we arrive at what let me down the most: the story. Now, as I said earlier, I absolutely LOVED the story up untill the second act. What happened after that, you might ask. Well, what happened was they completely and utterly thrashed a lovely and sad, but heartwarming story. Spoilers ahead. [spoiler]Throughout the first two acts we get to see how John and River got to know eachother, fall in love, get married, the troubles and whatnot they went through. Then we find out about Joey (what, to be honest, was more than expected at this point in the game) and the reason why John wants to go to the moon. All fine and dandy still. But then... They somehow manage to change his memories and make him [i]happier[/i] memories. The thing is, how is that a good message? All they ever did was present him with a comfortable lie which, although comfortable, is still A LIE. Instead of an inspiring story teaching us how life, no matter how troubling at times, is happy in itself and that we should all struggle to learn to enjoy our life as it is... We get a 'you done wrong, your life sucks because of some bad choices made for you when you were very young and you should be sad about it'... Which completely ruined the experience for me. Honestly, I was playing this game from beggining to end straight, without a single pause and right after the emotional crescendo which was the revelation at the carnival, we get this absolutely mindblowing idea that 'a comfortable lie is better than the truth'.[/spoiler]  I honestly wish the game had had a different ending. For me, it was a completely waste of time and emotions. [spoiler]Why should you ever feel sad at all? Simply construct a comfortable lie for yourself and everything will be fine![/spoiler]

That's only my opinion, of course, but sadly I cannot agree with this game, despite the hype.

I'm sure I'm going to get grilled on this review, but I honestly didn't like this game. I finished it because the reviews were so positve and I wanted to see what all the fuss was about. Now I know. It was not worth it. 

Pros:

The story was very thoughtful and original. I haven't heard of any other game, movie, book, etc that explores this last wish memory adjustment concept. It had an unexpected twist 3/4ths through and some feels. A++ for the story. That was the only thing that kept me going. 

The artwork was very well done, colorful, and overall impressive for the format. Personally, I do not like the sprite style. That was a hesitation when I bought the game, but I was willing to give it a shot. Nah, I just don't like it. If you like sprites, you'll love this. 

Music. Yes, the main theme is really nice. Generally the music supported the feels. 

Cons: 

The pacing was dreadfully slow. This game has almost exactly four hours of content. You can speed that up a bit by tapping through all the dialogue, but you can't speed up the ponderously slow panning, animations, walking, etc. Be prepared to spend some time just waiting because you don't have any other choice. 

This was a very story driven experience. The minigames were not needed and were just in the way most of the time. Its not like I got some sort of reward for solving them them faster or more efficiently so what was the point? I have enjoyed good minigames that added to the game experience - these did not. 

The navigation. So bad. I'm talking about just walking around. I shouldn't be blocked by a *small* plant if I'm trying to get across a half acre property. And the entire screen shifting suddenly to track with the player in the center. Because you could only move up/down or left/right, it was so distracting. If I tried to use the mouse to direct teh characters, they would not go farther than about 6 tiles without needing more direction. Why was this? The player controls and navigation were what I hated the most about this game. 

TLDR: 

If you want a sweet boy+girl story, you like sprite animation, or just want a low-impact diversion for a few hours, you may like this game. If you want something challenging or faster paced, this is not for you.

I was very disappointed with To The Moon. I spent around 3 and a half hours with this game, and only very rarely did I feel like the time was well-spent. The gameplay is virtually non-existent, player tasks boil down to point-and-click navigation through uninspiring environments to pick collect items placed sometimes in significant objects or conversations, and sometimes in random places that it's assumed you'll stumble over by chance. This is broken up by minigames, one repeating at the end of each sequence without becoming challenging at any point and the other one or two only appearing once each.

Basic gameplay is not necessarily a dealbreaker if the narrative and writing are good enough to provide an enriching experience. The reason I had picked up To The Moon in the first place was that I had heard tales of a compelling and emotionally resonant story, but I'm sorry to say the one I found was neither. The gist is you follow two main characters, whose job it is to reconstruct fake memories to bring comfort to terminally ill patients, as they meddle in the mind of an elderly man whose only regret is that he never went to the moon. It's an interesting premise which could raise interesting and profound questions. Is glossing over your real memories with ones that you think will make you happy wise? Are our choices and regrets something to be washed away, or an integral part of who we are?

In fairness, the final third of To The Moon does make a respectable attempt at raising these questions, but the characters through which it does so are neither interesting nor particularly likeable. The resonance of these themes and the story that is constructed from them rests entirely on how much the player has staked emotionally, and by the end I found that I didn't care what the outcome was. That combined with the fact that I found actually [i]playing[/i] the game fairly boring, meant that I really got very little enjoyment from the experience and would have preferred To The Moon to be lost in space, much like the last three hours of my life are.
