I honestly do not know how to feel about this game. I struggled for a bit on how to sum up how I felt. I needed to sleep overnight to really gather my feelings about it. It’s also hard to say exactly my thoughts in depth about the game without spoiling it, and I refuse to add spoilers into my reviews. For a game that is primarily story-based, I’ll attempt to do my best.

To the Moon is a visual novel made in the format of a cheap RPG Maker game. The artwork, I have to be honest here, doesn’t really look that good. It’s bland, cheap-looking, and doesn’t do enough to distinguish itself from other RPG Maker games. If I showed you this game without telling you what it was, you would simply think it was more RPG Maker shovelware. I won’t harp on this too much, though, because I think that it is absolutely possible to create art even in the form of something that looks cheap or indistinguishable from other games in the same engine. However, it is noticeable, which is why I bring it up. The music in To the Moon is stunning and beautiful. The main piano motif they use for River is fantastic. It’s moving, and really helps weave this emphasis into the game’s somber scenes, and it is a song that becomes synonymous with her. That seems to be by design, so good on them for that. 

The issue with To the Moon is the writing.

I was stunned when I learned that this game only has one writer when the credits rolled. Genuinely shocked. While playing through the entirety of To the Moon, it felt like two writers were clashing against one another’s styles. It’s as if they both wanted to tell different stories. The tone constantly shoots itself in the foot. The cause of this are the game’s two main protags, Eva & Watts. Without spoiling too much, their job is to essentially explore the memories of patients to grant them a last wish that they can experience in their mind during their final days. There’s more to it than that, but that’s the gist of it. Much of the game’s plot involves these two trying to help a man named John, who is on his deathbed, to reach his wish to go to the moon by viewing and altering his memories. This isn’t a big spoiler, this is information you receive within the first 20-30 minutes or so, let me live.

The problem is that Eva and Watts are terrible characters. Both of them show no empathy or sympathy for the events they’re viewing in John’s head, even when the events are depressingly sad. One could argue that they’ve seen many memories like this in the heads of other patients, and maybe that’s fair, but they don’t really show that in their personalities or display behavior that would point to that. Their dialogue is, and I don’t like using this word but it's apt here - cringe. Eva and Watts constantly behave like children for characters who are supposed to be in their late 20s or early 30s. They make needless pop culture references, and the game derails its own pacing at times simply to make unfunny bits involving them, such as one where Watts spends hours drinking at a bar with John in one of his memories. Humor is subjective, and you can argue they’re supposed to be the comic relief of the story. Sure. These are your protagonists though, in a game that is trying to deliver a message that’s really powerful and moving, but you have two morons who are essentially Jessie & James from Pokemon in terms of being goofy. Eva says things like “What the cucumber?” which is cringy in its own right, but even more so when you consider that characters in this game swear freely anyway, albeit the exact words being censored. Watts ridiculously references different media such as Street Fighter, Marvel, Dragon Ball and Doctor Who. (Huh, guess where the names John and River came from?) What is the point of writing these two like this? What, did you think the story was too ****ing dark or something? It’s not that dark, I’ll tell you that much. All of this quirky dialogue is off-putting, and takes you out of the experience. With all these depressing events they’re viewing, Eva & Watts come across as ***holes and childish for the way they react a majority of the time. 

Funnily enough, in some weird moment of self-awareness, Eva scolds Watts at one point for being a moron and says she’s “trying to get into this.” Me too! If you’d like another piece of dialogue from the game as an example of the writing, here’s an actual quote I noted because I was simply so baffled that I was reading it. Watts says early on, “Because we always succeed, because we’re awesome.” Ughhh.

It all really angers me - because on the other hand, To the Moon’s story around John and River is actually a narrative I want to love. There’s something here that is actually saddening to view. To the Moon has events that invoke something beautiful. Something meaningful, something remarkable, something special. Yet the writer insisted on butchering this beauty with amateur, piss-poor bottom of the barrel protagonists - with written dialogue that feels like it was written and forged in the Nine Hells of Ao3, by a 13 year-old girl with a Tumblr blog who’s never written in her life.

What’s worse is that To the Moon’s tragic story features a tale about a mental health condition that is worth telling. I won’t spoil what this condition is since it’s pretty important to the plot, but I know some people who would love to hear that they’re being represented in a game. All this quirky dialogue from Eva & Watts makes it feel like that the writer isn’t taking this condition seriously. It feels insulting, and that genuinely makes me upset and frustrated with the game’s narrative. Hence why I was shocked the game only had one writer. Why? Why would you do this? Why would you butcher and lobotomize your own narrative like this? You had something beautiful here, something meaningful that could really mean a lot to certain people, and it is simply utterly wasted.

I think an important and underrated facet of games is tone. It’s what allows a game like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta to coexist in a genre with Dark Souls, and in turn with The Witcher, or etc. If you can nail your game’s tone, then everything built around becomes woven together, like a perfect silk cloth. Not everything has to be a despair-ridden romp, that’s not what I’m saying. What I am saying is that your game falls apart when it has an inconsistent tone. To the Moon’s poorly conceived dialogue provides nothing of value towards forming its tone, and ultimately has a very inconsistent one throughout due to this. What an example to hear what I mean? It’s like if you sat down to watch an artistically beautiful  film like Forrest Gump, but you had someone right next to you on the couch the whole time cracking jokes and roasting moments of the film as if they were a Red Letter Media wannabe. That’s what it’s like.

I apologize if it seems like I’m harping on these two protags, but this is a visual novel. The most important parts of a visual novel are the narrative and dialogue. So when the dialogue gets unwoven by being so poorly-written, the tone of the game collapses. And when the tone of the game collapses, then so too does the house of cards the narrative stands upon. I don’t really recall a time where I’ve been this disappointed in a game’s narrative. It makes me sad because there’s something here with potential. It genuinely made me begin to tear up at times for certain scenes, albeit right before I was sobered back to reality by the rest of the writing. 

I’m also not sure why this is rated so highly either? Perhaps if you’re only a teenager or never experienced a proper narrative in your lifetime of “muh cozy games”, sure, maybe. I’m already in my seat and cozy, thank you. I want my games to give me something that’s worth my time, and To the Moon is simply not that. I do not recommend this game, even on sale, because I think there are better ways to waste 4 hours. Drive to Chick-fil-a or something instead, I dunno.

I had read a lot about how this game was supposed to have a great story, one of the best in modern gaming. I'm thoroughly baffled by these reviews. The level of writing of the game was on par with, say Final Fantasy 2. It read like a poor translation in a number of places and just had too many winks to other games. 

One of the main characters (you control one of two Rosencrantz-and-Guildensternesque scientists) is just constantly poking fun at things that are happening in the dying man's memories. It's as though the writer is trying to keep you from getting attached to the characters. A lot of the time the characters will start to explain something ("You mean you think it's...?") but then they don't finish their sentence, which makes you wonder why they bothered saying anything in the first place. The music struggles to keep the tone maudlin, but the writing will not give up its ceaseless buffoonery enough for you to invest any emotion.

Now that that's out of the way, here's what's wrong with the rest of the game: 

The controls are bad. They are minimal, so you'd think they'd be handled well, but no. You have the choice between keyboard or mouse. With you mouse, you can mouseover things to see if they can be interacted with. Unfortunately, the zones in which you place your mouse seem to be not placed well on the items they're representing, so you may need to move the mouse around to find them. Also, after clicking someplace to make the character move, the character may or may not move there, OR they may just stuff halfway there.

The keyboard controls are a little better, but you use the interactivity indicator, so you just walk up to everything that looks interesting and try it out. That wouldn't be so bad, but you walk very slow. Not all the time! Just most of the time. There doesn't seem to be any logic to when you can run and when you can't.

There are little puzzles thrown in that have nothing really to do with the plot. There is an "ideal" number of moves to solve each puzzle and a total number of moves you've made in all puzzles to that point, but once you finish the last puzzle, you never hear about those again. Irrelevant.

The plot has a gaping hole in the beginning, and there's really no reason why the wish can't be fulfilled at the get go, which negates the reason for the rest of the game.

The music is not bad, but it's honestly all kind of samey. It also doesn't seem to fit the mood in certain places, but how would you be able to tell anyway, again because of the writing.

This game should've been a film because all the interaction is either completely irrelevant or just poorly controlled. You're not going to glean any emotion from those tiny pixelated faces anyway, and the writing won't help you either. Pass this one up.

I went into this with decent expectations. I thought it looked like an interesting story from the trailers, and i had heard it had gotten pretty good ratings. But in all honesty, the game ended up just being a disappointment.

First things first, I'm gonna say the two things I liked about this game. The concept and the music. 

The concept I enjoyed quite a bit. A company that goes around giving dying people a chance to relive their life or alter their memories in order to give them a more peaceful death. Sounds like an interesting way to tell a story and can lead to lots of philosophical questioning about what it means to be a "self" and if rewriting the wrongs of your life leads you to a satified death. Could you rewrite your life so that nothing ever goes wrong? What will you have learned? The game never gets that deep though so don't worry about that. I don't hold that against it, that's something I personally find cool, but is most likely very hard to write about and probably can get a little too deep for a lot of people. Still the concept of editing memories is always a novel one to me.

The music definitely has some quality to it. Now I know everybody praises the music for this game, but I have to admit, while it's not bad, it's nothing really special either. When you finish playing the game there aren't any tunes that get stuck to you. Most of the songs are little piano diddies. They're more mood setter's than they are memorable catchy tunes. It ultimately comes off as generic piano music. Good music, but generic. Definitely nowhere near some of the best indie game soundtracks (ex. Bastion, Braid).

Now where does this game go wrong? I have to say its weakest point is the writing. Some points the writing is good. Usually anything dealing with Johnny (the central character whose memories you're walking through) is decently written. It can be sappy and is usually pretty serious, but it pulls off sappy alright. The worst writing, however, is usually between the two scientists (the characters you'll mainly control). There's just nothing believable about their interaction and it put me off quite a bit. Their relationship is an annoying case of silly guy + serious girl. It is very tiring and predictable. Here is a summary of most of their dialogue:

Guy: Makes a groan inducing joke purposely.
Girl: Respond with either: "..." or *bitingly sarcastic comment*

These characters are kind of supposed to be the comedic relief, but it never results in comedy, so there is never any relief. This set up is never funny, and it actually makes the writing feel very amateurish. The game also makes self referential jokes a little too frequently for my liking. They must've made fun of the main theme at LEAST 3 times, saying how it's repetetive. If this were the only fault then the story might be ok, but the sappy story is just that, sappy and not strong enough to hold everything together. Everything ends up being quite predictable (some little twists but nothing too crazy). None of the characters really grow or seem to learn anything. It's a love story that you've probably heard before with nothing new to tell you. Honestly, a lot of the writing sort of feels like an anime or something (which is to say, not that great).

The game is made with RPG maker so it doesn't look that great. That's fine right? I mean books don't have pictures most of the time and they can convey emotion and get emotional attachment. Sadly, the writing isn't strong enough to get you attached. I think what might've helped is if there were some hand drawn pictures to show some moments in the game. They do show a picture at one point, but that's it. Though you can tell that the quality of the picture isn't the best, so it's probably for the better that they didn't have much hand drawn art in the game.

Now some people would argue that this hardly a game. I don't wanna go down that route though. I would think that you should be able to tell from the trailers and such that it's not a very "Gamey" game. That being said, I think there is something to say about linear story telling in this medium. There are ways to do it and ways not to do it. You'd think with the premise of editing memories that the game would have a highly non linear aspect to it. Alas, the game does not take advantage of its concept and really doesn't take advantage of being a game.

That isn't to say that the game is completely devoid of game elements. You still have to walk around and explore and collect 5 or 6 orbs to move on to the next memory. You get orbs by witnessing events and clicking on objects in the memories. Click all the objects you're supposed to click and then you get to solve a little puzzle. The puzzles are simple and not frustrating. They can get a little complex but they never go anywhere too difficult. It's better that way because you really just want to move the story along, not solve puzzles, but this makes the puzzles just kind of seem like a time waster.

[b]TLDR[/b]:
     This is one of those reviews where a "mixed" rating would be more appropriate. However, since this game is pretty much universally praised, I'm going to be a bit of a contrarian. I did like the game but it left me with a bitter aftertaste that turns a timeless classic into what I would describe as a strong 6/10.

[b]The good[/b]:
     I think the main story is actually really good. I did think I would end up tearing up and even though I didn't, it is still a well written tragedy that pulls at your heart strings... at least for the time. I don't think it holds a candle to some other indie games that have come out since but it's easy to see why it was so acclaimed. The unique way of storytelling, the mystery that keeps you engaged for its, pretty short, runtime and all that wrapped in visuals that still hold up quite well. I've seen some people complain about how slow it is and while I agree that the walking speed could've been faster (or there could've been a run button), I think it lent itself to the story pretty well.

[b]The bad[/b]:
     ...I couldn't say the same for the main characters. The de facto point of view narrators are extremely dislikable and it only gets worse as the game goes on. I can excuse the outdated references and jokes that I simply didn't find funny but even without that they were easily the worst part of the writing which is pretty bad when they also get the most screentime. I get that having comedy relief is a good way to not make the experience feel too depressing but at times it really took me out of it. It's like watching a serious movie with a guy who scrolls through Tik Tok the entire time and keeps making jokes about the movie without actually caring about what's happening in it, and his friend who just as loudly keeps telling him to shut up.

[b]The ugly[/b]:
     Another big problem for me was the ending but I can't really discuss that without getting into spoiler territory so there's your warning:
[spoiler] I think the ending makes sense given the whole premise of artificially changing someones memory to make them think they lived a happy life but it's why I thought the moral of the story would end up being completely different. I can get behind the doctors wanting to fulfill Johnny's wish but after learning the context behind it, this bittersweet finale doesn't have any sweetness to it. The whole reason why he wanted to go to the moon (LAST SPOILER WARNING) was because of River. 
      This would be a fine motivation but the thing is that he already knew River in real life, even got married and stayed with her until death did them part. Johnny didn't know it but the real tragedy of his life wasn't that he didn't fulfill his own ambitions, it's that he forgot all of these memories, which she wanted to remind him of in her own way. With that said, the doctors should've asked Johnny if he actually wants to go through with the wish after actually knowing why he asked for it in the first place. 
     It's honestly hard to say if the artificial life he was given was even a better one, sure he achieved something big but it also cost him a lot of time that in the real world he spent with River. Would he actually want his memory to be changed into a fake fantasy or would he be satisfied with finally understanding why his house was filled with origami, knowing that in his last moments he would finally remember things as they were? Did he even expect that simply making himself believe that he went to the moon would come with these ramifications?
    I don't think he did and personally, I would much rather prefer knowing the painful truth over simply thinking that everything in my life went according to plan. If he thought differently then I would understand but we never get that answer, it was pretty much chosen for him and that just feels... wrong. Wrong in a way that I don't think was intended. [/spoiler]

[b]Conclusion[/b]:
I think this game is good experience for it's time that may not hold up as well as it used to. If you think this is a game for you then I recommend giving it a try as you might end up loving it. As for me, I just can't say I did.

This game has overwhelmingly positive reviews. I keep reading things about an "amazing and emotional" story, a "heart warming game", and "I cried". What?? I didnt get any of that after playing this game. It wasn't bad or amazing. I found it mediocre at best. Here's why:

[h1] Things I liked/enjoyed: [/h1]
[list]
[*][b] The Puzzles [/b] - To progress through the story, you have to solve a puzzle where you basically unscramble a picture. These puzzles are half the gameplay and one of the few "enjoyable" things about this game. Why did I like them? Because I'm the kind of guy who likes being stimulated by problems, puzzles, and challenges. 
[*][b] The Dialogue Between the Two "Side" Characters [/b] - These two characters aren't even supposed to be the main players in this "emotional" story. They are similar in purpose to R2D2 & C3PO from Star Wars where we see the story unfold from their perspective - but I still found their interactions more interesting than real main characters in this story. Imagine if in Star Wars, the plots were so boring that you had more fun watching the comradery and bickering between the two droids - that's how it felt for me here. 
[*][b] The Story Twist [/b] - This is the one part of the bland story that actually stood out for me and helped tie some loose ends. And yea, the twist is horrible and sad, but not tear-jerking.
 [/list]

[h1] Things I didn't have a strong opinion about: [/h1]
[list]
[*][b] The Graphics [/b] - Pixel graphics are used here. They're alright - I don't love them or hate them. They don't take away from or add anything to the game. It is what it is.
[*][b] The Walking [/b] - This is the other half of the gameplay. For the most part, you walk around in order to witness conversations and find objects. Sometimes, there's a lot of walking. Pretty simple and the main point of the game is the story anyway, so I'm neutral on this.
[*][b] The Life Story of the Main Character [/b] - I found it generally meh. It was just a means to progress the game. And by that I mean the story was uncovered bit by bit before me and I observed it with the same amount of professional detachment that a physician shows when he checks your gonads during your routine physical. 
 [/list]

[h1] Things I disliked/got annoyed with: [/h1]
[list]
[*][b] The Music [/b] - Most people who have played the game would say "What?! The soundtrack is the best part!!!!!" Well it wasn't for me. Sure, the piano soundtrack started off nice. In fact, I liked it in the beginning. But then as the game went on, the same few tracks kept looping over and over and over and after a while I was getting real sick of those sickly sweet melodies. When I was halfway through the game, I was trying to rush to finish so that I wouldn't have to hear the music anymore. The biggest relief I had was when the story became more dramatic which in turn played the more dramatic music. But afterwards, it went back to the sickly sweet. 
[*][b] The Broken-Up Story [/b] - The real problem of the storytelling is that I couldn't even feel invested in the story because it kept getting interrupted by the dialogue between the two comic relief characters! Their interactions seriously distracted me from the so-called sad story going on. The mood of the story was supposed to be serious but then there were jarring interludes of snarky jokes and punchlines that reminded me of the Lab Rats show from the Disney XD channel. It got to the point where I stopped caring about the main character's sob story and cared more about the dynamic between the side characters. 
[*][b] The Main Character Himself [/b] - *Spoilers* [spoiler] The main character does something in his teenage years that I actually got pissed at. He wants to ask the girl (his future wife) out and his friend cautions him, saying something along the lines of "she's slow". The main guy doesn't care, but his reason for wanting to date her is literally something like this: "I don't want to be the same like everyone else, I want to be different. So I will date someone who's different". Wtf? What kind of stupid hipster reason is that? He wants to date her [b] because [/b] she has a disability? Who the fuck does that? If you date someone with any disability, it's because you like him/her [b] despite [/b] the disability, not because of the disability itself! He didn't wanna date her because she was nice, interesting, funny, cute, or whatever. Only because she was "different". He eventually marries her for reasons not clear to me and when they're old, it just seems like he's frustrated and simply tolerating her. What a load of fuck. [/spoiler]
 [/list]

[h1] Minor Things I thought were pointless: [/h1]
[*][b] The Puzzle Moves [/b] - Each puzzle has a moves "goal" which is the minimum number of moves needed. This seems interesting but what's the point? There's no incentive to get the goal as far as i can tell and there's no score being kept throughout the game. 
[*][b] Tense Situation Between Side Characters [/b] - Towards the end, the leading side character does some action without telling her partner (and us) why. The partner gets angry and frustrated and for some time tries to demand answers. What was the point of doing this? We find out later thatthe lead side character wasn't doing something bad, and I saw no reason why she couldnt have shared her solution with her partner. In fact. they were in contact throughout the whole ordeal so what's the point of keeping him (and us) in the dark? Just seemed like a cheap attempt to create a tense situation. 

[h1] Final Verdict [/h1]
Overall, it was an okay experience where the side characters were the most enjoyable parts while the music was the least enjoyable part. All the aspects that I've listed more or less balance each other out, so I give this game a rating of 5/10. Whatever emotional impact or deeper meaning the game had or could have had was lost on me because of the storytelling and the story I couldn't care too much about. A lot of reviewers say this game taught them the importance of choices and consequences and stuff like that and made them reflect on their own lives. Well this game definitely taught me that too, as in, it made me wish I could go back and spend those 6 hours on a different game.

[h1]Buy this only if you care about story more than gameplay. A [u]LOT[/u] more[/h1]

[b]Story[/b]
The story is, definitely, the strongest point. You play as two cientists working for a corporation that alters a dying person memories in order to artificially grant their last wish; in this case, Johnny, that wants to go to the moon. The way the story is told is amazing; you go from recent memories to more distant ones, and this creates mistery upon mistery that gets solved the deeper you go. You'll also find out more about the relationship between Johnny and his wife, River, and how much his life changed because of it, as well how their plans and dreams turned out in the future.
You will always want to know more because the misteries keep piling up, and feel touched and conected with the characters and their problems - both very real and well developed. The amazing and sentimental soundtrack helps to create this atmosphere.
Sadly, those are the only good points.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is awful. Starting from the menu screen: you can't alter the resolution. Yup, this only runs on a ridiculous 640x400 resolution, and on full screen there's these huge black borders (it was released in November 2011; there's no excuse). Yuck.
To make it worse, the graphics are way outdated. It was supposed to be that "pixelated old school" look, but they are horrible and bad looking, with a tiny and way too bright color scheme.
To top it off, you'll hit invisible walls constantly. Sometimes you can go through bushes, chairs, logs and narrow paths, other times you can't. And there's no way to know until you try.
To proceed further in the memories, you have to solve some "turning titles" mini game that has no reason to be there. Oh, and even though it says it has controller support, it doesn't.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
To The Moon has an excelent story, told in an original and intriguing way, with unique and believable characteres, but the gameplay and graphics are so horrible that you end up getting frustrated as you play (I couldn't play more than 30 minutes at a time), compromising the beautifull story.

At first I read the other reviews talking about how wonderful this game is and how the dialogue is phenomenal and will make you sob playing it. I can assure you that this is not true. There are few instructions of how to move around in the game, meaning that it took me until nearly the end of the game before I realized I could use arrow keys to move the main characters rather than pointing and clicking the location for them to travel. The actual minigames within this are incredibly easy, such as finding items as mementos to travel through the man's memories, and this puzzle that you have to complete before travelling. It propels you along a linear story line with very little help from the player besides moving around through the map. The pixel graphics are good for their type and age, but when it comes to the dialogue, it is horrific. The dialogue appears in text boxes, and sometimes the dialogue wasn't fully in the box to be able to read. Through about half the game there was a way to make the dialogue automatically appear rather than scroll as the character is speaking, but then this option was disabled, meaning you have to watch every useless strand of dialogue appear on the screen. The dialogue itself, while it has previously been praised, is about on par with a Wattpad fanfiction writer, and uses many colloquialisms in the speech (and sometimes not even colloquialisms, but just slang that you may only use in text messages or bad stories on the internet). While I admit that the plot is a tear-jerker, this is simply because they throw additional plot twists in here almost as if it is a drama on TV, not because it makes sense in the given context. Pretty much, the story only makes you cry because they just keep adding sadness for the sake of sadness. Much of the dialogue doesn't make sense realistically, and the humor is awful. I should start by mentioning that I first heard about this game through a YouTuber named "TheMysteriousMrEnter." He's used music from this game in his videos and credited the songs from the OST. I looked up the game itself, and I initially thought this was going to be an homage to JRPG's from the Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis era, like Undertale. The game itself makes a small joke about that, pretending to start up a turn-based battle, but then they just move forward.

I will say, first and foremost, that I enjoy the narrative and presentation. The graphics, while simple, use a lot of muted colors and a low resolution to create a realistic atmosphere; the music is beautiful, especially the main theme, "Everything's Alright."

The premise is an interesting idea, where two scientists, Eva Rosalene and Neil Watts, work together to alter a dying man's memories, to fulfill his wish to travel to the moon. As the game goes on, you see what sparked this motive, and the life he and his family had over the years. There's also several unexpected turns that leave you guessing how this man dealt with tragedies and grief that occurred in his life, and what the scientists will do to achieve their mission. I was about to HATE the ending when the female scientist went off by herself to alter the man's memories in a certain way, because it meant the man would completely forget about a huge chuck of his life, one that he should be able to remember; but then I see how she replaced his memories, and the payoff at the end, as well as her actions, felt justified.

So what's my problem here? The gameplay, or lack thereof. As I mentioned, this is not an RPG like I was expecting; it's an adventure game where you solve puzzles and use the man's memories to, in a sense, travel through time. You can't go all the way back to his earliest memories in one "memory hop", you have to perform numerous backwards hops over the course of the man's life. You do this by finding a "memento", a concrete object from the man's memories, which have to be activated using 5 "memory links", other objects and small details in the background found by combing over a contained environment. When you take the memory links to the memento and activate it, you solve a simple puzzle, which is flipping all the tiles to form a picture of the memento. You have to do this process at least 7 or 8 times, while watching the story play out; it gets just as repetitive, and sometimes confusing, as finding a certain number of magical glowey things in a 3D platformer to unlock the next stage. Once you've done this process enough times, you have to link the mementos together in a chain so the scientists can go back to the man's earliest memory, alter it, and set a butterfly effect into motion, thus fulfilling his wish.

But that's just Act 1! The second act of the game involve the scientists finding alternative methods to go all the way back to the man's earliest memory, which they can't immediately access; the third act of the game is watching the earliest memory, followed by a disjointed climax where Dr. Watts has to chase down Dr. Rosalene who goes off on her own to alter the man's memories, without explaining the plan to him. Throughout all of this, there's 5 or 6 detours that the scientists have to take to solve problems, and the solutions they come up with are sometimes nonsensical. 

Again, I like the narrative of this game, but that's just it: this story doesn't work as a video game! The gameplay, while interactive, is so minimal, that a single playthrough just becomes a tour through set pieces, automatically moving forward in a straight line at a certain pace. The most freedom you get is talking to NPC's and looking at certain objects in the contained environments. This should've been a graphic novel or an animated movie, because it feels disjointed and bogged down as an interactive medium.

Even the two free "minisodes" are just really short epilogues where you're wandering back and forth through the building where the scientists work.

Speaking of them, another problem I have is the two scientists as characters. Dr. Rosaline and Dr. Watts spend the WHOLE GAME constantly bickering and trying to one-up each other over the course of their mission. It's fine if they're not best of friends, or they disagree on how to go about the mission, but they don't even act professional or civil with each other; it's just mindless fighting and word games between these two. They obviously need to be there as protagonists, and they shouldn't just be blank slates, but when I follow a pair of grown adults acting like children fighting on the playground, and I have to watch the story unfold from their perspective, it ends up bringing down what's otherwise a beautiful story about seeing a dying man's dreams come true. Imagine going to a large, elaborate wedding, and you have to sit next to your two friends who spend the whole ceremony yelling at each other in the back of the venue; that's my metaphor for the scientists in this game.

So I unfortunately can't recommend this game. Watch a "Let's Play" on YouTube to experience the story, and then buy the soundtrack on the developers' Band Camp page, instead. You'll actually get more out of it that way.

TL;DR: If you like sad stories, play it on mobile instead. If you're looking for actual gameplay, skip it entirely.

To The Moon is a good short story with some pretty piano music, unfortunately told through a bad game on a terrible engine.

Gameplay-wise it's essentially a point-and-click adventure where each stage ends with one of those little "flip the tile" puzzles. Even though there are only a handful of puzzle images, some of them are used repeatedly. Nothing about the gameplay is very fun, it's just a vehicle for the story.

Some of the art is jarringly low-quality, while the rest of it looks like it might actually be good if it there were any way to set the resolution or adjust the scaling. Instead, the low-res pixel art suffers from forced fullscreen with resampling that just makes it look like a blurry mess on my 24" display at 1920x1080.

Not only are there no graphics settings, there are no settings of any kind. You're stuck with the high mouse sensitivity and wonky controls that cannot be reconfigured (for example, at one point you're moving with the arrow keys while holding spacebar to move faster, but still using the mouse to hover over and click things.)

I haven't played the mobile version of the game, but I see that there is one, and I can only imagine that that would be a much better experience. Bad scaling and bad keyboard/mouse controls would both be a total non-issue on a small touch screen, and the short, digestible chapters and simple gameplay seem well-suited to mobile.

The writing is just plain atrocious. There's no two ways about it. All characters (save for one neurodivergent girl) are mean, unlikeable, inconsistent, and make no sense. All their dialogue is either forced, incomprehensible, or both, and save for like two jokes that were actually funny, it's full of "humour" that makes you want to punch the wall. At almost no point does the story move in a direction that makes the least bit of sense, and most of it is so bafflingly mean and pointless that you're left wondering what the point of it even is. For a long while it seemed like it was going to be about learning to live with an autistic spouse, which would be a great angle for unique story with a purpose, but no, in the last act she's thrown under the bus too in the meanest way imaginable. Also all the "progression" in the story is based entirely on characters not explaining and/or listening to anything, and it's obnoxious beyond compare. This COULD have been a really good story, if it were written by someone who knew what they were doing, or at least ran it by someone. We kept waiting for it to get good, playing through the awful parts we hated, but it never did. Sadly, the game only has awful parts we hated.

The gameplay is perfunctory at best, with sluggish controls and annoying "puzzles" that are just there to be in your way. Most of it is cutscenes anyway, but you're just forced to "control" the characters (except you don't actually have any control over any outcomes) all the time, and it's annoying. The game should really have had one button only, "advance the dialogue", and nothing else.

Graphically the game is fine, it's a typical retro-looking RPG maker fare. In some places it's inexplicably not pixelated, which is jarring, but it's fine overall. The music is actually really good, and the main theme is great (even though every single character rags on it in-game for some reason). It's the one single thing in the game that was genuinely enjoyable with no reservations. Too bad it's embedded in a game that makes you hate it, and hate what it could've been but wasn't.

Dr. Wyatt and Dr. Rosaleane are scientists that can recreate memories in order to enable dying people a chance to live out their final request through their dreams. As the game starts the pair arrives at the house of a dying, elderly man whose last wish is to visit the moon. In order to grant this wish they must travel back through his memories to discover the roots of his desire.

Whether or not you enjoy To the Moon will depend entirely on whether you become invested in the story of a dying man and his last wish of going to the moon. There is virtually no 'gameplay' to speak off and, aside from a few simple puzzles that bookend each memory, players will spend most of their time just clicking on objects in the game world in order to progress whilst listening (well reading) the conversations of the NPCs. There aren't even any decisions to be made like there are in games such as The Walking Dead.

Fortunately however the story, while in some ways clichéd, is heartfelt and a real step above what you'll find in most video games. At around four hours long it is also just the right length to ensure it doesn't out stay its welcome.

To the Moon won't be for everyone, I can certainly understand some of the negative reviews, but those after a more sedate and thoughtful experience should give it a try. 6/10

I was baited by the "overwhelmingly positive" reviews on Steam and it needs to be acknowledged that the story is emotional and deserves all the praise. But that's about the only positive this game has. Despite being a story-driven game, it's not justified if the game play is clunky and if the protagonists (that have 80% of dialogue) keep interrupting an otherwise smooth immersion into a heart-gripping tale. 

The puzzles are repetitive and get monotonous rather quickly as little is to be achieved from tile-inverting minigames. The pixel graphics may be good to look at, but with invisible barriers everywhere, it's a dumb click-fest just to get your character to move where he/she needs to so the story can progress. 

The protagonists are apathetic and constantly taking a jibe at the journey of the man whose dream they are supposed to be fulfilling which defeats the whole purpose of the story. The music is decent but the negatives of this game outweigh the positives which makes it impossible to recommend that someone pay money for this lackluster excuse of a video game. If you want to buy, make sure you pick it up during a sale, full price is undeserved. 

I may be in the minority in not recommending this game; I have no hesitation in paying for a 5-hour game focusing on a good story but if I had to drag myself just to get to the end and if the game itself feels like a chore, the payoff is not worth anyone's money or time no matter how good the story is.

Sometimes all a narrative game needs is a good story and you can forgive the faults. However, To The Moon has everything going against it despite having a very unique and interesting story.

The dialogue is quite bad. At some times cringeworthy, and other times just missing the mark on a joke/reference. It feels as if the author knew the destination for their story, but didn't put enough effort into how the characters would get there.

The music does all the heavy lifting. Due to the terrible dialogue, the game relies on the amazing soundtrack to carry you through the story beats. This is the biggest strength of this game because the music completely nails every setpiece. I'm confident if they removed every line of dialogue from this game, used only emotes and sprite work, this would be a knockout.

The controls are frustrating. Since you are really just walking around in this game, easily moving your character around should be a top priority. However, your character advances too many steps in a button press, leaving you to run into many walls because you overshot.

A very unique story dragged down from the sum of its faults.

As a rule I am apprehensive about walking simulators. At worst they are just novels that you turn the page by pushing enter. [u]To the Moon[/u] has nothing that makes either a traditional video game or walking simulator any good. It is a tedious game with a nauseating sob story; something a clingy girlfriend might force you to watch. Except this time there's no payoff you might get from placating a spouse. 
Like most walking simulators there isn't anything one could call gameplay. You manoeuvre characters through environments. You talk to characters or look at items to progress the story. The most complicated gameplay loop in the game goes something like this: Look at some items, pick up some marbles, shove them in a glass bubble, smash the bubble open by solving a 2D Rubik's cube, then proceed to the next area and do it again. It's awful, and at no point was I having fun. The game teases us by having a modestly deep inventory system, and even a real-time ECG of the old man's heart; and then uses none of it to make for more interesting gameplay. 

But people aren't praising this game for the intense, strategic gameplay; it's all about the story. So what is the story?
A dying man's brain is infiltrated by 2 technicians who try to rearrange his memories to send him "To the Moon", but it's really a narrative of a guy meeting his future-wife with some tragedy sprinkled around. This ain't Tolstoy. It's not even Bronte. This is some kind of perverse low-rent Danielle Steele. There are many eye-rolling references to things like Mice and Men and Ani-morphs (whatever that is). None of them work, it just feels amateurish and you'll be begging this to end half hour through, but you'll have 3.5 hours more to go.

Not saying they would have really helped that much, but it's illustrative of the product you're dealing with.

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

TLDR: A walking simulator that guides you on a cruise around an existential horror if you actually pay attention. 

Oh boy. This one is a lot to unpack. Its odd review time again, because this is… this is something. So let’s dive into it. 
Framed as a romantic and heart-warming short story, To The Moon is a pixel walking simulator interjected with a tile flipping mini-game that adds literally no value, and a couple of other poorly controlled minigames that just aren’t very interesting or fun. You play as a pair of doctors for an end of life service that go into dying people’s brains and alter their memories, so that they achieve a single dream they had throughout life. 
The idea, the potential, the protagonist doctors, and the way the story is told and unpacked are all so well done that they make the experience quite pleasant… but there is something deeply wrong with the story in and of itself that I will get to.

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Deep characters that are well thought out, have their own motivations, unique personalities and relationships, and stay true to their world views. 
[*] Emotive story that is well told, with fitting music, and decent pixel art to go along with it. It made my cold dead orbs glisten once, brought a sad smile to my face, and made me laugh my brittle, dusty, laugh out loud at least once.
[*] The potential for this to become an *actual game* is huge. There were clearly plans for expansion throughout and I guess it was cut down to meet what was possible. I hope someday they’re met.  
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The mini game is pointless. It plays out like it might do something and ultimately doesn’t. There is no consequence for taking 100 turns if you want, nor 1000. Nothing changes or is added.
[*] I felt like the game promised the moon (hurhurhur), teasing me with mysteries to unpick, paths to follow, and a time based mechanic that would only allow me a few actions per session so everything would count. 

It delivered a spam click and move around using poor controls mixed with minigames that also use poor controls. Were the story not so powerful this would be a major problem. 
[*] The lack of agency. 
This expansion deals with this in detail, it unpicks the ending of the game as well as character develoments, so be warned. 
[spoiler]Firstly, let’s look at the ending. We get no say in whether or not River should be erased in her current form. This is problematic in the sense that I agreed with Neil, not Eva.
Secondly, let’s look at what that eraser [i]means[/i]. They completely erased his life to allow him to build a delusion. It was to fulfil a last wish, yes, but does that make it morale? Was it even his actual wish? What if they were petty or vindictive people? Could anyone have known what they really did? What happens with the data of the constructed person? Is the Johnny that’s a read only program, really read only? What does it mean to be sapient? Is that facet just a program? Or is it real? Could it tell? If the program is a construct using brain base data to create a reality around itself to make a life, what separates it from a biologically constructed person? The morale implications are quite vast.
Finally. Let’s talk about River. The beauty lost in this is more tragic than anything else. [i]River knew. [b]She. KNEW.[/b][/i] Through their entire lives, she knew who he was. Exactly who he was. But he didn’t. We’ll never know if she knew he was a twin that lost one, or if she accepted the Joey/Johnny grandma link. We’ll never know if she worked that out, or pulled together [i]why he’d forgotten her[/i]. But she spent years building a constellation of rabbits to try and bring him home to her. To show him that she remembered the first times, that it was more than just teenage angst. She chose a spot with its own fucking light house for Christ’s sake, trying desperately to signal to him, to remind him of who he was. And she kept the platypus for what? 60 years? Eva missed the point. And destroyed it all because of wording. No delusion could have ever been as powerful, or meaningful, as John remembering, understanding, and appreciating the beauty of what River tried to give him, in her own way. Neil knew this, and understood what “I want to go to the moon” really meant. Robbing us of the chance to take him to the moon he wanted deep down was an absolute travesty, and swaps the story from being a touching and sombrely beautiful tale of missed opportunities and missing connection into an existential horror where the person who loves you most and is desperately trying to bring you back to yourself is erased, their efforts ground to dust and then thrown in your face as a façade of merriment so you can die without the guilt of not understanding them [i]when you could have changed it so that you did in the first place[/i] 
[/spoiler][/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]

 [list][*] Remove the minigames that add absolutely nothing to the game. 
[*] Expand on the mysteries and puzzle solving stuff. There’s an entire house to explore in the present, and an entire life to explore the history of, it would have been a lot of fun if you could jump in and out, forward and back, and use the things around the house and his memories to try and unlock the passages to the next sections by filling in his memories with the data around them… possibly making mistakes along the way, changing the outcome of the story. 
[*] Provide multiple endings, based on spoiled changes. 
[/list]

1. This game isn't good. Sorry you had to hear it from me.

2. W/ that out of the way, the music to this is stellar, absolutely on par w/ the very best game soundtracks of all time. No kidding. Go to Freebird Games's Bandcamp page. Buy the album, skip the game. Win/win. 

3. Even the presentation beyond the music is fine. It's done in an old school pixel art style, which is pretty cute even if it doesn't feel all that fresh these days. But even how these simple graphics are done reveals the kind of lack of attention to detail that makes this game a chore to play ultimately. It is  640x480 natively and there is no way to change that. It upscales just fine and I don't mind 4:3 w/ bars on the side of a modern monitor but on top of that, for the majority of gameplay, there is typically a black bar both on the top and the bottom of the window as well. The end result is only about a quarter of the available real estate on a normal screen is being used at any given time and since sprites are already pretty small, things are needlessly hard to see. Lots of games get an old-school feel in 16:9 so I just don't see the reason for this design decision. It is not a dealbreaker on its own but it is just the kind of thing [i]To The Moon[/i] gets wrong over and over.

4. The controls here are pretty bad too. There is controller support but mouse and keyboard works better, which doesn't really fit w/ the bit-era aesthetic. I can live w/ that but the controls are weird and wonky anyway. I constantly found the mouse pointer getting sort of stuck on a previously clicked object and would report the same bit of dialogue no matter where else I pointed at the screen.

5. One of the small challenges presented (intentionally) by the game designer was essentially a pixel-hunt so number 4 gets really annoying. 

6. The other small challenge is these tile flipping puzzles for the first half of the game which are either really simple or can be solved in a matter of minutes by trial-and-error. 

7. All of the above technical limitation could be forgiven in such a story driven game, which leads us to the real kicker. The story here is really, laughably bad judged by the standards of any medium but video games. Again, sorry you had to hear it from me. 

8. The premise is a pretty solid sci-fi trope along the lines of "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" or [i]The Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind[/i]. There are two technicians who have the ability to somehow actively enter into a person's memories and change them for fun and profit. In this case, this astounding technology is used to improve education and fuel scientific development into even more amazing technologies... Wait, no, it's used to make dying people feel better for the last few moments of their lives by manipulating them into thinking they did things they didn't do. Hooray for science!

9. Predictably, our two technicians run into some pretty unusual things when exploring this dying patient's head-space. Unfortunately, the presumably reliable details of this poor fellow's past are odd enough that it makes it difficult to suspend disbelief--and this is after you've swallowed the idea that people can act as video game characters in another person's brain box. It is hard to explain w/o spoilers but, in my opinion, a hefty majority of the backstory presented would occur only if every actor in it were insane.

10.  There is one joke in this that is actually funny.

11. Even w/ everything wrong w/ it, the story would not be so bad were it not told in such a painfully slow manner. The pixel hunt sections I mentioned in 5 can span multiple screens and really fill up a lot of time. I think this story could easily have been a short story that might take an hour to read and the game is going to take most people 3-6 hours to finish. The game play really adds no challenge and the story is completely on rails so your choices don't add anything to it. I just can't help but feel a game was a really bad choice of medium in this case. It might have made a great comic book. 

12. Right at the end, [i]To the Moon[/i] almost redeems itself w/ an ending that would seem to drive home a valuable life lesson but then takes a hard turn into a swamp of sticky-sweet sentiment and happily gets mired there. I guess if you liked the plot up to that point, this is what you'd want.

13. So here we have it: great music, problematic design choices, poor controls, unbelievable story, unfunny humor.  One could be forgiven if they thought this whole game wasn't just a brilliant soundtrack subjected to death by a thousand cuts but it is somehow not a total disaster. I have spent a lot of time thinking about it since completing it which is something I can't say about a lot of games I actually like. Unfortunately, I am mostly thinking about how no plot points jibe w/ how normal people actually act in real life.

Think about [b]To the Moon[/b] as an interactive [strike]novel[/strike] modern fairytale. Although, it's made with [i]RPGMaker[/i], it's a quality work. The artstyle and soundtrack are beautiful. There are no major technical problems, except for the low resolution due to the engine used, lack of [i]Steam[/i] overlay and, hence, a lack of an option to take [i]Steam[/i] screenshots, as well as an extra launch window in the background. I should also note that the game uses the same type of puzzle over and over again. The puzzles don't complement the story and are there only to fill the time between dialogues and scenes.
Anyway, the game's main selling point is the story. It focuses around a dying man's last wish to go to the Moon. Your goal is to find a reason for this wish and grant it by planting a memory inside his brain. It is accomplished by a special machine that allows you to travel through other people memories as in a virtual reality. It's a good concept for a story, but everything else - not so much. The story is supposed to be a tear squeezer, and there ARE good emotional moments in it, but more often than not it made me cringe due to the overload of cuteness and sentiment. It doesn't shy away from cliches, neither. And the dialogues are something that an 8th grader would write.

If there was an option to give a neutral rating, I would give this game a neutral rating. But, since there is no such option and I didn't really enjoy it, I give it a "thumb down". However, I am aware that there's a niche for such games. If you enjoy Disney classics or sentimental fairytales, then this game might be for you. It could also be worth your time, if you're considering purchasing [i]RPG Maker[/i] and want to see how a popular and high quality game made with this software would look like.

To the Moon follows two scientists exploring the memories of a deathbed patient with the objective of essentially implanting a new memory.

The game is divided into three acts. The problem is that the first act is just awful. The second and third acts salvage the game a little bit, but it's not worth your time in my opinion.

The first act is by far the longest. Of the 7 hours I spent on the main game (the two DLCs were each 30ish minutes), I would say I spent four hours in Act 1. Act 1 is comprised of the scientists going backwards through the patient's memories. To reach the next/earlier memory, you must find 5 "memory links" that you can then use to activate a "memento." This is the game's downfall in my opinion and why I can't recommend it.

The "memory links" are random items that can be found throughout the memory. Finding these memory links felt like a chore to me. Oftentimes, they didn't seem to be related to the memory. Clicking on them usually spawned a line or two of dialogue from the scientists or occasionally from the characters in the memory, but sometimes they did absolutely nothing except get logged that you found them. At no point did finding them feel rewarding or like I had any real direction on what I was looking for. Most of the time I felt like I ended up dragging my mouse along the screen looking for any sort of indicator that I was hovering over a memory link. I'd click it and maybe it would be a memory link, maybe it wouldn't be. Sometimes the links were items, sometimes they were conversations, sometimes they were sub-memories within the memory, sometimes they were vistas, sometimes they were interactions between other characters, etc. But not every conversation was a memory link and not every item was a memory link. It wasn't a challenge, it just became "have you clicked everything in the memory yet to find all of the memory links?"

Once you did find all of the memory links, you then had to find the memento. Usually this wasn't difficult but I did get frustrated trying to find one or two. Then you have to click the memento five times so that all of the memory links fly into the memento, then you click on the memento again to activate it, then you do a tile puzzle game with the memento that has absolutely no relationship to the game as a whole, then after you solve the tile puzzle game you click the memento again to open another menu so you can click again to use the memento. After doing that about 20 times, it gets horrendously tedious.

Frankly, the memento aspect felt like the developers felt like they needed to add some "game" to their game and forced it in. The "game" (tile flipping to reveal a picture of the memento) just doesn't belong. It is completely jarring to suddenly face one of those puzzles after some emotional scene.

Eventually, everything got annoying to me. Movement became annoying. Movement is point-and-click. You can't hold the mouse button to make the characters continue moving in one direction. There's no option to make movement into WASD. There's a segment at the end that changes movement to the arrow keys and then uses WASD for something else (besides movement). In a 2D game, WASD felt so natural and intuitive whereas mouse controls just didn't. Pausing is done through right-clicking. It's such a small, almost silly thing to complain about, but it just goes to how much I didn't feel comfortable with almost any part of this game.

The story didn't salvage it for me. I didn't like it, but it wasn't *bad.* Unfortunately, it just didn't hit the emotional high points for me that everyone else raves about. Sciency memory alteration aside, it's not very unique. To be honest, I'm not neutral when it comes to the story. By the time the story actually got any legs under it (act 2), I was already very over this game and just wanted it to end. But I'm the kind of person that is going to play it to completion if I bought it.

Act 2 and 3 are better, but they're short. Both almost fully abandon the memory link/memento junk that completely ruined Act 1, although it comes up briefly again somewhere in there.

All in all, I can't recommend this game. This is a story that wanted to be a game, not a game with a story to tell. There are better stories to spend your time on, better games to spend your money on, and better experiences to spend your effort on.

To the Moon is all about its story, so therefore I will not summarize the plot apart from this: the story is about two doctors trying to fulfill a dying man's last wish of getting him to the moon.

As mentioned, the focus with this game and its greatest selling point is the story. The plot is pretty good; it has a few twists and the way the doctors try to help their client is interesting and well written. Also, the characters have real depth, which is the more impressive as To the Moon lasts but a few hours.
However, the story is also completely linear, the player is never presented with a meaningful choice and the levels are really small. Furthermore, the game tries to deliver an emotional experience but as you - due to plot reasons I cannot explain - are an outsider for the majority of the game the things happening on screen sometimes fail to deliver said experience; there is too much detachment.

Gameplay is threadbare and consists for the most part of walking to location/person X and clicking through (sometimes quite a lot of) text. These grant orbs that you need to combine with an item you need to find, after which you need to solve a very simple puzzle to continue the game. Repeat the above for almost every level. As mentioned, the levels are very small so you spend the majority of the time reading the dialogue. The gameplay fits in with the story, though.
What's worse, gameplay is bugged. The characters sometimes don't respond (well) to clicks and sometimes get stuck. Moreover, the mouse is rather imprecise during the puzzles and that is annoying as it leads to more missclicks.

In conclusion, I feel this game has nice characters and at its core a good plot but it lacks choice for the player and the story is completely linear. On top of that, it has bugged, threadbare gameplay that gets really repetitive a few levels in. Due to this, I cannot recommend To the Moon.

I really wanted to like this game.  I saw the rave reviews, the story sounded interesting, as did the largely 16-bit inspired visual style and beautiful music.  I love sci-fi, point and click adventure games, classic RPGs (for the stories at that), and if there's feels involved, bring it on.  It should have been easy for me to like this game, yet there were several things that got in the way.  Before you continue, please understand that I did actually complete the game in spite of my frustrations, as I had heard the ending must be experienced.  

Negative:

Gameplay - (or lack thereof): The game itself is by far the worst part of "To The Moon".   There is no way to lose or get a game over, and the entire experience is as linear as it gets.  Considering the genre this isn't a deal breaker for me; I can accept an artistic indie game as an alternate means of storytelling.  But it was when it tried to be a game that it became stressful.  For the most part, each scene revolves around finding artifacts in a hidden object type fashion, while at the same time watching more of the story unfold.  After each scene, you're required to solve a panel flipping puzzle before moving onto the next scene.  You are given a minimum number of moves as a goal but then left to solve it with no reset or undo button, so if you end up making too many wrong moves it becomes less a solveable puzzle and more a matter of random clicks until you eventually can move on.  These became easier for me as I got used to them, but no less unnecessary and frustrating.  Other than that there is a very short stage that plays a little more like an action game but it is clunky and sloppy, which makes me wonder why it was even included.  There is a short little whack-a-mole mini-game near the end that was probably the most it felt like it was a game.  The rest of the time, well I hope you like clicking the mouse and reading.

Controls: The graphical style might evoke a nostalgic factor but I couldn't help feeling that a top down RPG style might have been the wrong choice here.  Using the mouse is clunky at best, and object textures are often randomly placed, blocking your path when you least expect it.  There is no run button, so much of the time spent was slowly walking place to place.  Discovering the arrow keys and spacebar was a lifesaver but there were still times I went to the mouse for ease of clicking on key items and characters.  

Writing/Dialog: In a game almost entirely carried by dialog, it felt like there was way too much of it.   The bickering siblings dynamic between the two main characters got old fast, and their conversations often felt immature and sarcastic.  There are moments of clever comedy but they are few and far between.  However there was no shortage of shameless nerd culture references if you like that sort of fourth-wall breakage-I found it annoying for the most part.  


Positive:

Story: While coming off a tad pretentious at times, it was a solid yet often predictable feels-fest.  Through all the other aforementioned issues I had with the gameplay, I still wanted to find out how the story resolved.  I wasn't disappointed, but I wasn't surprised either.  

Graphics and Sound: The music is beautiful and always fits the mood, and the graphics are attractive and familiar.  

Summary: For me, To The Moon lacks the necessary substance to be defined as a video game.  Instead it is a little 3ish-hour interactive story with plenty of sentiment and pleasant graphics and music.  Gameplay is easy, yet made unnecessarily frustrating by an overabundance of filler dialog, annoying minigames that feel like an afterthought, and generally clunky controls.

Gameplay must be used to enhance the story or even completely tell it, otherwise the plot's impact would be just as effective, if not more so, in a different medium. The few times this game actually gives you control it is nothing special, some walking and event triggering, or a painfully simple puzzle that's tied to the current scenario. To The Moon, like many other games, uses gameplay as a roadblock between you and the next story event, causing a stop start flow to the narrative and gameplay. It would have made a good short film or short story but I simply did not enjoy To The Moon as a video game.

Not sure if that's the idea that the writers want you to come away with, but I suppose there IS some value in pondering that.

But there are also some pieces of the plot which don't seem to fit, and a bunch of moments when the characters are difficult for me to relate to.

For 4 hours of "play", I'd say the price is about right at 85% off.

In the heyday of any fledgling medium vying to be taken seriously, advocates tend to get a little trigger happy with setting off the congratulatory fireworks. Any effort - so long as it is, indeed, an [i]effort[/i] - will find itself inundated with roses and champagne, as every able-bodied critic joins the ferverous parade to go suck its d*ck off. This is why the largely inconsequential bullsh*t that makes up [b]Uncharted[/b] gets to be "cinematic", why the uninspired, postmodern-lite [b]Dr. Langeskov[/b] gets to be "clever" - it's pure wishful thinking. 

[b]To the Moon[/b] is a nice effort. The indie flood gates hadn't quite opened up in 2011, so I forgive the critics, the fans, hell, even the [i]creators[/i], for all the undue hype. There was little else at the time doing what it did, and so, as an inovator, as [i]trendsetter[/i], the game certainly shined for its ambition. Games like [b]To the Moon[/b] should be encouraged, and encouraging games like [b]To the Moon[/b] in 2011 led to a dev community that gave us [b]Dear Esther[/b], [b]Gone Home[/b], and [b]The Beginner's Guide[/b], but make no mistake: [b]To the Moon[/b] sucks.

The game tells the story of a man who lived a lacklustre life and, on his deathbed, wishes he could have gone to the moon (roll credits), so he conscripts the help of two WHACKY scientists to go into his brain and construct those memories for him. [b]Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind[/b] by way of [b]Ivan Illych[/b], I guess. Whatever. The more traditional "game" aspect largely just exists as a vehicle for what is an otherwise pretty weak YA novella - "play" is experienced through transparent scene-padding, consisting of scavenger hunts for arbitarily determined objects of "sentimental signifcance", with each section to be advanced by completion of a sliding-block puzzle.

When a game relies this heavily on storytelling, it's imperative that that story is a) a good one, and b) well told (often, in a game, through clever mechanics). [b]To the Moon[/b]'s story, on the other hand, is high school amateur writing bad. The exposition is delivered non-stop through some of the hammiest dialogue I have ever been subject to. Every character is an effusive faucet of their own thoughts and feelings, each rendered in such painstaking transparency as to its narrative or emotive purpose. "OH BOY, THIS PLOT DETAIL SURE IS MYSTERIOUS, ISN'T IT?" Kan Gao loudly shrieks into my ear as I play, "OH BOY, I BET YOU'RE SURE GONNA GET FEELS WHEN THAT PAYS OFF!" Well, no, actually, I won't, because you broadcasting every move you're going to make really softens the blow of these punches you're supposed to be landing.

GameSpot awarded [b]To The Moon[/b] the honour of "best story" in 2011. Comparatively, the New York Times warned readers that they would be "intermittently guffawing and constantly [...] amazed by a succession of surprises in [b]Breakfast at Tiffany's[/b]". These are growing pains within an industry that is coming of age, nothing more.

I was very late getting to this game, and the reviews and praise had been out for several years before I got to play.  So I was expecting great things, I was expecting to be crushed by the end of the game, I was expecting an amazing soundtrack.  I was expecting-- something fun, at least-- out of the gameplay.  None of those things were delivered.

Why make a game out of this?  Is this the best medium to tell your story?  Is your story even worth telling?  The premise is that an old man full of regrets effectively wants to cancel his entire life on his deathbed through memory manipulation.  He dies with false memories.  Would you rather die knowing the truth, or die in a lie, ignorantly blissful?  Now thats an interesting question, but it was completely ignored by the game creator who unequivocally sides with the lie.

Its cool that games want to be art.  There are not many games that strive to be.  But you can't just praise a game because its one of few that tries to be something greater.  If this was a book or a movie, if the soundtrack was a standalone CD, if the game was simply a 2D puzzle game without any art, it would be completely criticised in EVERY aspect.

Ultimately this game is a waste of time unless you just want to see where the indie game industry is trying to go.  If you're looking for a thoughtful story, beautiful art and music, all wrapped up in an interactive video game, you might be disappointed.
