This is not a game in any real sense. While it is “interactive” in the sense that you move around the environment and interact with objects, in truth the interactivity is an illusion; yoru movement in the environment is about as interactive as turning a page in a book most of the time, and at times is actually more tedious because you have to search for where you need to click to get to the “next page” – in the case of this game, the next bit of dialogue or cut scene. The only real “game” elements it contains is a single game of whac-a-mole towards the very end – which you do not need to succeed at to progress in the game, and which actually has no impact on the game at all, as far as I can tell – and some simplistic tile-flip puzzles which are present for the first third or so of the game. These feel wholly out of place in the game and are simply discarded later on. There is no possibility of failure in the game, and the one section that might feel remotely “game-like” is mostly just tediously walking down a hallway for about five minutes – if that. In the end, it is much closer to a movie than anything else – and most likely, should have been exactly that.

The story ultimately has four main characters. Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts are the two primary protagonists of the game, and are who the player controls throughout the length of the story. They work for the Sigmund Corporation, a corporation which specializes in rewriting the memories of dying people so that they can experience a different life in which a single wish comes true. The way this is accomplished is by entering the minds of the dying person, viewing their memories, and going back to their childhood and implanting a very strong desire to complete whatever one wish they wanted to see; because they would have a singular, powerful drive their whole life to achieve that goal, their mind will simulate them succeeding at that task (most of the time, anyway; it is implied that it is not foolproof, but that it is pretty reliable) and they will live out their dream in their mind before dying.

The inspiration from [i]Inception[/i] is obvious, but the game itself has a very different take on things; the goal, in the end, is very different, and the Sigmund Corporation is paid to by the dying people to grant these mental wishes. We immediately see that Dr. Neil Watts is the funny, goofy, eccentric guy, while Eva Rosalene is the competent, no-nonsense character; even still, both have their moments of seriousness and comedy, and Dr. Neil Watts is definitely a Jerk with a Heart of Gold type character, who tries to cover up his soft spots whenever he does not absolutely have to do so.

The dying man in question, Johnny Wyles, is being tended to by his housekeeper, Lily, whose two children run around the house. Early on, I thought that Lily and the children might play some sort of significant role in the story, but in the end they’re only bit parts; the real major players are Johnny Wyles and his deceased wife, River Wyles. As we go back through time via Johnny’s memories, we see events unfold in reverse, and come to understand why things ended so badly for Johnny and River, and why Johnny was unhappy with his lot in life in the end.

The story, on the whole, is reasonable, though there are a few strange plot-holes – for instance, River dies because they cannot afford to pay for both her medical treatment and the new house that they’re building, and River believes that the house is more important than her life, but somehow, Johnny can afford to have a full-time caregiver live in his house, as well as afford presumably expensive end-of-life treatment which allows him to achieve his dream of going to the Moon – something he himself does not even understand, and which the player only learns the true reason for very near the end of the game. The final memory sequence throws a different cast on many of Johnny’s other memories, and it was neat to see how they’d incorporated the hints as to what had really happened earlier in the game.

That being said, I was actually a bit disappointed by the game’s true ending because, unfortunately, I came up with a much better plot twist partway through the story. The first time their attempts at implanting the memories failed, I went back to view Johnny as an old man and the memory was exactly the same. However, there was something which was very interesting which immediately caught my eye – Johnny could not explain why he wanted to go to the Moon, which was seen as unusual by the two doctors, and supposedly made their lives much more difficult.

It was at this point that I realized their brilliant masterstroke – the reason Johnny had no idea why he wanted to go to the Moon was because they (or someone else) had implanted the idea that he wanted to go to the Moon, and thus it felt like an unnatural desire which was simply foisted off onto him that made him feel compelled to wish for it in the end.

I was severely disappointed when it turned out that this was not the case, and the actual cause for it was very different. It wasn’t a terrible reason – even if it was a bit cutesy and a bit clumsy at the same time – but it just didn’t stack up to the plot twist I had built up in my head, and thus I ended up feeling a bit disappointed by the revelations of the true ending of the story.

In the end, the story took a fairly long time to get through, and I got the feeling that it would have made more sense as a movie than it did as a “video game” – moving around in the environment was mostly unnecessary tedium, and the game at times went into cutscenes which showed that it could have simply been a movie the whole way through. It would have gone by a lot more quickly, and likely been several hours shorter as more of a visual novel or movie-like experience, and I think I would have enjoyed it more as such. The pacing was a bit of a problem in places, particularly towards the end when Eva sets everything up for the grand finale off-screen without explaining it to Neil (and thus, the player), creating some unnecessary tension between the two for no good in-character reason. The sequence could have been greatly shortened, made much more visually interesting, and it still would have worked; instead, it felt weird and unnecessarily drawn-out.

There were also a few moments of extreme strangeness. Perhaps the greatest is when the characters at the start of the second act of the story, unable to figure out how to get Johnny to want to go to the Moon, start bursting into Johnny’s memories at random to pitch the idea of going to the Moon to him. While the characters at this point are very sleep deprived, the mood whiplash in this section of the story is severe, as went from some fairly serious memories with humor thrown in to lighten the mood to frenetic comedic action on the part of both of the protagonists. While the humor which was interspersed into the rest of the game actually worked pretty well, the humor in that particular section felt off and too extreme; it is never mentioned again afterwards.

All that aside, the core of the story worked well enough, and while it wasn’t as good of a story as the one I made up in my mind about halfway through the game, I can’t say that I disliked it or felt like the game cheated me, and am interested in seeing if they do something else interesting with the characters in the future – the story ended with the promise that it was “Episode 1 – To the Moon” and, while the story of Johnny and River was tied up in the story, Neil and Eva, our scientist protagonists, have more patients to deal with and more things to do. I’m interested in the idea of seeing what else could be done with them, but I'm not sure I want to spend five hours instead of two watching them do it.

To the Moon is a bad video game and a bad story.

Before you flame me please note that my issues with the game extend past its rudimentary gameplay, poor graphics, and nonexistent settings. Also note that I have played several games similar to To the Moon which I will shout out in my review. If you're looking for a good adventure game, just going off of stuff I've both played and are available on Steam, check out the Ace Attorney Trilogy, Zero Escape: The Nonary Games (999 specifically, as that game is fantastic), killer7, or VA-11 Hall-a, and there are loads of other games I haven't played that seem better than this (Telltale's The Walking Dead, Danganronpa, Firewatch, 428, all of the LucasArts games, etc.). Hell, if you're looking for an Adventure game built in RPG Maker, I'd highly recommend OFF over To the Moon, and that game is [i]free[/i] (I have also heard good things about Yume Nikki and Ib, but again, haven't played them)

So let's address the obvious problems everyone already mentions. This game was built in an old version of RPG maker, which means a few things. First off, there are no settings to speak of, so I hope you like playing the game fullscreen with a low resolution, and I also hope you like clunky controls with inconsistent movement speeds. The graphics are also super generic. This isn't even a limitation with RPG Maker, OFF was made in this engine and that game has actual character design and an aesthetic protrayed in its worldbuilding. This is probably controversial, but I don't like the OST, there's a ton of piano songs and while they do provide a moody atmosphere, they largely blend together. As someone who loves video game music and will gladly seek out the music of games I've played, I really have no desire to do so with To the Moon. This is especially hilarious considering one of these piano pieces is a major story element. Once again, OFF had an atmospheric OST, but it was farrrr more unique and thus compelling to listen to on its own (on an aside, I adore its usage of [spoiler]Somewhere Over the Rainbow[/spoiler]). The gameplay basically boils down to running around a clunky RPG overworld to find certain interactables and solving some extremely basic tile puzzles…hell you don’t even play tile puzzles by the end of the game. 

So we're left with one thing: The narrative. The story itself is mostly compelling and has a cool setup: Look through a terminally ill patient’s memories and change them so that they remember themselves being an astronaut and going to the moon before they die. It has a very moody atmosphere and the story at least gives good payoff to the things it sets up. However, the overall tone is suuuuuper melodramatic, like it's actively trying its best to make you sad or emotional because of the music and the events we see the characters go through. But...I honestly don't care about any of that, because the characters and writing are quite poor. The characters are bland as hell and lack much in terms of personality or anything interesting; I can’t recall the names of most of the cast, and I have very little to say about the ones I do remember. While I can tell you about Johnny's life and what he goes through, I can't say anything compelling about him as a person. He uh...likes olives? He wants to go to the moon? His relations to other characters don't matter when they're ridiculously uninteresting: River and Johnny's mother's characters have some good idea but ultimately they aren't enough. The two leads have personality, but they also totally break the game’s serious tone with some really cringe-y writing that sometimes devolves to just referencing things, and it often becomes obvious that this was an indie game made in 2011 (Doctor Who references? Really?). I know it makes sense narratively since this is just another day of work for them, but it doesn’t make for an entertaining experience. And again, they really don't do much beyond that, they don't have any character relations outside of themselves (not even with Johnny tbh), so I don't really feel anything for either of the two leads. Compare them to some of my favorite characters, Phoenix Wright from Ace Attorney and Gillian from Va-11 Hall-a. They are very silly and entertaining characters, yes, but they also have a number of fun and interesting relationships with other, similarly deep members of the cast (Maya, Mia, Edgeworth, and Larry; Jill, Dana, and many customers and randoms), on top of their own depth like Nick's backstory and his motivations to be an attorney, and Gill's connections with Va-11 Hall-a's themes of coming to terms with your past and focusing on the present. To the Moon's characters just don't have any of that...

At least the story, in terms of the events taking place, is good for much of the game…at least until the climax and ending which are [b]awful[/b]. It's both nonsensical and RIDICULOUSLY emotional manipulative. I imagine the devs want you to cry during this sequence, but I was absolutely livid. To get into spoilers, [spoiler]how the HELL is River the one preventing Johnny from going to the Moon, the loss of his brother and subsequent loss of his memory is the real thing keeping from doing so. There is absolutely no reason for her to have been moved to a later part of Johnny's life, and the fact that your partner REFUSES to explain anything while doing this is, also, nonsensical and only serves to add tension through that chase sequence. And then, they segue into this ]emotionally manipulative disappearance sequence with a disgustingly sappy song...ONLY THEN does the game back-pedal on River's disappearance because of course it does, it obviously wasn't going to commit to rubbing out River, the game just wanted you to cry for a bit. Sigh..,I'm not against emotional story moments, but please don't force it and let it make sense (i.e. 999's S*f* Ending). Not like it would've mattered much in this case since, again, I don't feel much of a connection with these characters to begin with. Also, while I'm on story spoilers, the twist that Johnny has a twin brother is pretty dumb[/spoiler]

When I took all of this into account, I realized something…To the Moon has [i]nothing[/i] going for it. The graphics are mid, the gameplay is mid, the soundtrack is mid, and they even managed to botch the story. While it wasn’t a straight-up pain to play throughout, I can’t say I came out of this game with a positive outlook.

If you legitimately cried at this game, I'm glad you were able to find an emotional connection that I couldn't. But also, I'm sure there are plenty of other games that will make you cry harder.

First thing’s first: To The Moon is not a game. I hesitate to call it a “story,” and it certainly isn’t a work of art. Reading the “Overwhelmingly Positive” reviews makes me feel like I’m out of the loop on some elaborate prank to make me feel insane.

Most obvious from the store page; the graphics. They’re RPG maker graphics. Nothing special, but aside from some… questionably drawn scenes, it’s basic pixel art. That being said, the utilization of said pixel art is dull. Everything is bland with drab colors and samey design, which is a huge problem because of…

…the “gameplay,” if you can call it that. Drag your playable character around with awkward, clunky movement controls and click on every random object in a dull room until you find the one insignificant thing the developer decided you HAVE to interact with to progress. While a handful are signposted okay with visual cues that guide you toward them, the vast majority are just senselessly chosen and placed to pad out the already painfully slow pacing of the “game.” In addition to this, there are randomly scattered puzzles, many completely unrelated to the plot and with poorly designed arbitrary solutions (For example, there's a random Animorphs trivia question that doesn't even have the correct answer).

But, let’s be real, none of that matters, right? To The Moon is about the AMAZING story that sets a NEW STANDARD for what games should be, right? Wrong. Wrong in a million ways. There is hardly a story here to tell, despite what the reviews will tell you. The first three quarters of the game is a mindless slog with zero substance and the least likable or interesting characters you will have ever seen. You have the two “witty” scientists who serve only to undercut any even slightly serious tones the game comes close to building. The main character (the old man in the bed, not the playable characters) has zero discernible personality. The main character’s wife, aka the OTHER main character is a caricature of someone with autism; she’s totally incapable of expressing herself in any way (unless the plot calls for it and she all of a sudden does a complete 180), and her whole personality is just being a rude smartass because she has autism; a complete spit in the face to anyone who actually has ASD.

The game is a disjointed collection of the main character’s memories, as he has asked the player to enter his mind and implant fake memories of being an astronaut because he wants to go to the moon. About three hours in, the developer must have realized he’s done absolutely nothing productive with the story, because out of nowhere the final quarter of the game turns sharply into an ending almost completely disconnected from everything else. The last hour of the game is another, faster-paced series of random events, but this time with poorly written and repetitive emotional music playing over it. The game is so desperate to claw an emotional response out of its audience that it’s honestly laughable, and does not earn a single one of its attempted emotional moments, though I assume the general melancholic tone of much of the game is what drives people into thinking it’s deep when it’s really not doing or saying anything at all. 

Overall, the game is just a mess, and has virtually zero redeeming qualities. I cannot recommend it for anyone to be honest, and especially today there are dozens to hundreds of well-written, beautifully crafted masterpieces that respect your time, money, and brain much more than this garbage ever could.

I enjoy story-driven games, especially ones with emotional weight and unique narrative structure. To The Moon definitely tries to be one of those—but for me, it didn’t quite land.

This game is a novel, a very interactive one, which is great! You walk around as Eva and Neil, piecing together memories and playing through a handful of puzzles and minigames.

Honestly? The best part of the game was the doctors. Eva and Neil are genuinely fun characters. Neil’s bad jokes actually got me chuckling, and I loved all the little references and unexpected scenes that came with them. They were the heart of the game for me—I found myself more invested in their banter than the main storyline.

Now, the story...

It’s told backwards, which can work well in certain games or films—but here, it made everything feel a bit predictable. It's a string of explanations instead of a gradual journey to a grand finale.

Despite the constant reminders that “John is our client,” I couldn’t help but focus on River. All her quiet efforts to make John remember. It wasn’t his fault, of course. His memories were buried too deep. But it felt like River never truly got a chance to be understood.

And that ending...

Spoiler ahead.
[spoiler]In the end, River got to the moon alone—despite everything she tried to do to reconnect with him. It broke me a little. Not because it was tragic, but because it felt unresolved. Unfair.[/spoiler]

So, while I can see why To The Moon resonates with so many people, it just didn’t hit me the same way. The characters had charm, and the concept is genuinely touching—but the execution left me feeling distant.

[h2]Story and characters[/h2]

As the blurp says, you play as two doctors who go backwards through a dying man's memories to artifically fulfill his last wish. That sounds great, but in practice it means that you visit scenes from this man's life that were significant to him but, in-game, you are just an observer, it is all very surface-level. You do not interact with the man or the other characters (with very few exceptions), you can't really investigate anything, you are just dropped into the scene, read a few lines of dialogue (no voice-over), and that's it. 

At one point, you manipulate his memories, and then skip through his life events again, this time in the right direction, to see how this manipulation affected his "life", and if you managed to "fulfill" his last wish. But, and there lies the main problem for me, it does not actually affect anything. It manipulates a dying man into misremembering his whole life (on his request). What you see didn't and does not happen, and could not have happened in reality. 

It is a bit sad if you think about it, but you do not get to know any of the characters well enough to get emotionally invested, at least in my opinion.

The memory scenes are presented through the eyes of the two doctors, who are the real protagonists, and I found them pretty much insufferable. They were clearly intended as comic relief, and they are constantly squabbling in a mean-spirited and at times childish way. I think there's supposed to be a romantic undertone but the inane dialogue completely ruins it. 

[h2]Gameplay and the rest[/h2]

The actual gameplay consists for the most part of you dropping into a scene, trying to find the very few points that you can interact with, and collect five "memento" points and a core memory. If you have found everything, you can leave the scene and have to solve a mini-puzzle. It is always the same type of puzzle, and it is neither difficult nor fun. 

There is no indication which parts of the scenery are walkable and which aren't, and there is no logic behind the mementos, so you are randomly clicking everywhere to either move somewhere else or find one of the mementos. 

This is even worse in the few "action" sequences, in which you can run around with the arrow keys. There is no excuse for having such buggy and clunky controls even in a game from 2011. 

[h2]To sum it up[/h2]

Currently, the game is tagged as "emotional". In my case, that emotion is annoyance.

I do not recommend this game.

I was told I would love this game. On paper, I should. A narrative game, practically a walking simulator that touches some big themes, like life and death, disconnect between loved ones, human life's fragility, and so on. People told me they cried. I love games that make me cry.
This one didn't.
It tried, by throwing at me beautiful music and sentimental scenes. Problem is, these scenes weren't earned. You can't have a big payoff scene without an equally big setup, and the story that comes before that big climactic scene where you're supposed to cry... Well, that story just isn't good.
This is the story of a dying man's life, and we go through it scene by scene. Unfortunately, after spending trwo hours going through his memories I didn't really learn anything about him, and had very little reason to empathise. The game shows you a bunch of disjointed scenes from a man's life that don't come together. In the end, I still didn't know what kind of person he was, and I still wasn't sold on the meaning of the game's central metaphor. 
In the end, going to the moon didn't really matter, no matter how beautiful a final scene it was.

SUMMARY: 

Can you imagine walking around Final Fantasy 6, watching the story unfold without any gameplay? Without any RPG? That's exactly what To The Moon is. Can you imagine walking around Myst and Riven, listening to someone narrate the story wtihout any puzzles that perfectly integrate into the story and environment? That's Dear Esther. Gameplay would only serve to enhance the experience and story, just like it did in FF6, Myst, and Riven. These developers were either too lazy or stupid to realize how gameplay would enhance what they were trying to accomplish. 

FULL REVIEW:

To The Moon is an example of a devolution in gaming. To The Moon is an example of video games giving less; degenerating into a worse state than what games have been in the past. 

Unfortunately, many act as if To The Moon is some revolutionary, innovative experience. It is not. It is the exact opposite. 

To The Moon does tell a very good (not classic, but very good) story. The story is original, which is more than most Hollywood productions can say. The characters are relatable, deep, and funny at the right time. The dialogue is well written. The plot twists are very well done. The music is remarkable. 

Yet, as I went through the story, I felt empty. I had this same feeling playing through Dear Esther. Everything I said above was also true about Dear Esther (To The Moon is basically the 2D 16-bit version of Dear Esther's approach). 

Then I realized why I felt empty.

Every positive point about To The Moon I said above -- story, characters, dialogue, plot twists, music -- I had already experienced almost 2 decades earlier in Final Fantasy 6 except that -- FF6 actually had gameplay. And everything I experienced in Dear Esther I had also experienced almost 2 decades earlier with Myst and Riven except that -- Myst and Riven actually had gameplay.

THAT is the problem. To The Moon is incomplete and lazy game design. To The Moon did what FF6 (and so many other 2D games) already accomplished in terms of story-telling -- which is fine, but the developer of To The Moon was too lazy or too blind to understand that gameplay is an essential part of gaming (and that gameply can actually enhance the story and experience like it did in FF6, Myst, and Riven). Instead of implementing gameplay into To The Moon that could enhance the experience and maybe make the story even more impactful, the developer chose to just have us walk around the world and watch the story unfold. 

Can you imagine walking around FF6, watching the story unfold without any gameplay? Without any RPG? That's exactly what To The Moon is. Can you imagine walking around Myst and Riven, listening to someone narrate the story wtihout any puzzles that perfectly integrate into the story and environment? That's Dear Esther.

These are not games. They're interactive stories. And maybe if they called themselves interactive stories, I wouldn't be so harsh. But they don't. They stomp their feet and yell they are games. But they are not. They are interactive stories told by story tellers that, for whatever reason, didn't want to be bothered with implementing actual gameplay around their story to make it...ya know...a game. To the Moon and Dear Esther are ultimately empty, half-experiences that do half of what Final Fantasy 6, Myst, and Riven did two decades ago. They are an example of the devolutionization of "games" (HINT: because they're not games).

[h1]Great Story, but Frustrating Design Choices[/h1]

To the Moon is more of a slightly interactive visual novel than a traditional game. It’s entirely linear, and while you have an inventory, it’s essentially useless and only serves to push the storyline forward.

One major frustration is the lack of options to override the super-low resolution and non-widescreen format. You can press Alt+Enter to switch to a small windowed mode, but it’s still far from ideal—and you'll need tools like Windows Magnification to make it somewhat bearable.

The tile-flipping puzzles, while a neat idea, suffer from input lag, causing clicks to mis-register and leading to unnecessary frustration.

That said, the story itself is quite compelling, and if you’re a fan of narrative-driven experiences, you might find it worth pushing through the design flaws. But, these issues can detract from the overall enjoyment.
